subtopic: PERMANENT COURT OF INTERNATIONAL JUSTICE, OPTIONAL CLAUSE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PERMANENT COURT OF INTERNATIONAL JUSTICE, OPTIONAL CLAUSE
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the declaration under article 36 of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice, signed at Geneva in respect of the Dominion of Canada, on the 20th day of September, 1929, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution asks the approval of parliament to the signature of His Majesty's government in Canada of the optional clause of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice, which was signed on behalf of Canada at Geneva on September 20 of last year. I understand that the approval of the honourable the Senate has been given this signature, and that this optional clause also has been approved by His Majesty's government in Great Britain and has been signed by all the other dominions of the British Empire. As a charter member of the League of Nations Canada accepted the obligation set forth in article 13 of the covenant as follows:
The members of the league agree that whenever any dispute shall arise between them which they recognize to be suitable for submission to arbitration or judicial settlement, and which cannot be satisfactorily settled by diplomacy, they will submit the whole subject matter to arbitration or judicial settlement.
Disputes as to the interpretation of a treaty, as to any question of international law, as to the existence of any fact which if established

would constitute a breach of any international obligation, or as to the extent and nature of the reparation to be made for any such breach are declared to be among those which are generally suitable for submission to arbitration or judicial settlement. For the consideration of any such dispute, the court to which the case is referred shall be the Permanent Court of International Justice, established in accordance with article 14. or any tribunal agreed on by the parties to the dispute or stipulated in any convention existing between them. The members of the league agree that they will carry out in full faith any award or decision that may be rendered, and that they will not resort to war against a member of the league which complies therewith. In the event of any failure to carry out such an award or decision, the council shall propose what steps should be taken to give effect thereto.
This article provides a description of classes of international disputes which are to be regarded as justiciable, that is to say, suitable for decision by a court applying rules of law. But it does not impose upon the members of the league any actual obligation to have such disputes settled in this manner. The original draft of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice contained a provision giving the court compulsory jurisdiction in the classes of cases set out in article 13 of the covenant. In the statute as adopted by the first assembly this was replaced by a provision which appears in article 36 of the statute. It is as follows:
The members of the League of Nations and the states mentioned in the annex to the covenant may, either when signing or ratifying the protocol to which the present statute is adjoined, or at a later moment, declare that they recognize as compulsory ipso facto and without special agreement, in relation to any other member or state accepting the same obligation, the jurisdiction of the court in all or any of the clauses of legal disputes concerning:-
(a)	the interpretation of a treaty;
(b)	any question of international law;
(c)	the existence of any fact which, if established, would constitute a breach of an international obligation;
(d)	the nature or extent of the reparation to be made for the breach of an international obligation.
The declaration referred to above may be made unconditionally or on condition of reciprocity on the part of several or certain members or states, or for a certain time.
The terms of article 36 have been regarded as admitting the making of a reserve or exception of any kind when accepting the compulsory jurisdiction of the court, because the jurisdiction of the court may be accepted "in all or any" of the classes of legal disputes enumerated.
It will be recalled that article 2 of the treaty for the renunciation of war as an

Permanent Court-Optional Clausa
instrument of national policy, to which Canada is a party, provides that:
The high contracting parties agree that the settlement or solution of all disputes or conflicts of whatever nature or of whatever origin they may be, which may arise among them, shall never be solved except by pacific means.
This treaty, however, does not provide any machinery for the pacific settlement of disputes. As regards disputes of a justiciable character, therefore, it is possible to consider signature of the optional clause as the logical consequence of the acceptance. Acceptance of the optional clause means that disputes falling within its terms will receive from the Permanent Court of International Justice a definite solution which the parties to the disputes are bound, under article 13 of the covenant, to "carry out in full good faith." If the pact of Paris is to be made fully effective, it seems necessary that the legal renunciation of war should be accompanied by definite acts providing machinery for the peaceful settlement of disputes.
His Majesty's government in Canada has given its careful consideration to this matter for some years past. The Canadian government notified the secretary general of the league in 1925, that it was ready to consider the acceptance of the optional clause.
It will be remembered that at the Imperial conference of 1926, the following agreement was reached by His Majesty's governments there represented:
A general understanding was reached that none of the governments represented at the Imperial conference would take any action in the direction of the acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the permanent court without bringing up the matter for further discussion.
Such "further discussion" was begun on the initiative of the Canadian government in February, 1929. It was actively continued during the months preceding the tenth assembly of the League of Nations, and reached its conclusion at Geneva when Great Britain, the dominions, and India decided to sign the clause forthwith.
I think this outlines the material points with respect to this matter.

speechtext:
On September 20, 1929, five days after the Irish Free State had signed without reservations, representatives of Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India signed the optional clause subject, mutatis mutandis, to the reservations set out in the following declaration:
On behalf of His Majesty's government in Canada, and subject to ratification, I accept as compulsory ipso facto and without special convention, on condition of reciprocity, the jurisdiction of the court in conformity with article 36, paragraph 2, of the statute, for a period of ten years, and thereafter until such time as notice may be given to terminate the acceptance, over all disputes arising after the ratification of the present declaration with regard to situations or facts subsequent to the said ratification, other than:-
"Disputes in regard to which the parties to the dispute have agreed or shall agree to have recourse to some other method of peaceful settlement, and
"Disputes with the government of any other member of the league which is a member of the British Commonwealth of Nations, all of which disputes shall be settled in such manner as the parties have agreed or shall agree, and
"Disputes with regard to questions which by international law fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada,
"And subject to the condition that His Majesty's government in Canada reserve the right to require that proceedings in the court shall be suspended in respect of any dispute which has been submitted to and is under consideration by the council of the League of Nations, provided that notice to suspend is given after the dispute has been submitted to the council and is given within ten days of the notification of the initiation of the proceedings in the court, and provided also that such suspension shall be limited to a period of twelve months or such longer periods as may be agreed by the parties to the dispute or determined by a decision of all the members of the council other than the parties to the dispute."
As to the effect of the reservations contained in the declaration of signature:
The declaration follows the usual practice in being subject to reciprocity and including a time limit. This is fixed at ten years, but the acceptance continues in force after the expiration of the period, unless notice is given to terminate it.
The signature is also subject to ratification which will enable the question to be raised in parliament before the acceptance of compulsory jurisdiction comes into operation.
The declaration covers only disputes which may arise in the future. Past disputes and disputes relating to past events may be submitted to the court under a special agreement concluded in each case.

This statement, I think, covers the matters asked for by my hon. friend and gives to the House the information it will wish to have before it at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking for myself, I
do not think that this house should hesitate in passing unanimously this motion for the ratification of the revised protocol relating to the establishment of the Permanent Court of International Justice, and also speaking for myself I agree with the statement as to conditions and reservation on behalf of the Dominion of Canada which has been read to the House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
As I understand the reservations, they embrace three classes of cases. The first class in simple language, covers disputes between Canada and any other country, which countries may agree to settle such disputes in some other way than by an appeal to the permanent court of international justice. The second class covers questions or disputes between this Dominion and the motherland, or any other self-governing dominion of this empire. The third class covers disputes which may arise between this country and any other country upon matters within the jurisdiction of Canadian courts and which are being settled in the ordinary courts of Canada or of the other country involved. Unless the proceedings in such courts are suspended, in cases falling within these three classes there shall not be an appeal to the Permanent Court of International Justice. I consider these reservations reasonable and proper, and subject to them we are prepared to accept the compulsory jurisdiction of this court.
I think we all understand that the permanent court of international justice is an outcome of the Treaty of Versailles. It was constituted in the year 1920 with the formal approval of this government as well as the formal authority of some fifty other self-governing countries of the world. We have had almost ten years experience of this tribunal and as is the case with all human structures, from time to time some defects have been discovered which were not perhaps anticipated when the structure was originally set up. According to the belief of most people, the greatest weakness in this court has been the fact that until very recently one great country of the world had never given its adherence to such a tribunal, that country being the United States of America. One de-
[Mr. Mackenzie King.)
feet if I may so call it, has always existed in the League of Nations itself. It has been the fact that the United States never became a party to that league. Another weakness is the fact that another great power of the western world, Brazil, although originally a member of the league has subsequently withdrawn. In Canada we find ourselves in I he position that while we are members of the league and have taken a very active part in its transactions, two other great powers of the western hemisphere, although signatories of the Treaty of Versailles are not now members of the League of Nations. That is undoubtedly a defect and a weakness in the League of	Nations but	in its wisdom	theLeague of Nations has decreed that although certain nations have not become formal members of the league, it was still open to them to participate in the Permanent Court of International Justice. Until recently the Lnited States had not become a member of this	tribunal, but I	think it was	inthe	year	1923 that	the President	ofthe	United	States sent	a message to	the
Senate recommending that that country become a party to the permanent court. After a year or two of consideration by the Senate of the United States, it was resolved by that body that, subject to certain reservations, the United States should give its adherence to the International Court of Justice. I think it was in the year 1925 that notice of that resolution was communicated to the League of Nations and the league very promptly took the matter into its most serious consideration. It is true that one of the reservations demanded by the United States was a matter of great importance and I have no doubt the consideration of that reservation gave a good deal of difficulty to the League of Nations at the time. But after the fullest consideration of the question by a body of men who might be called experts in the matter of international and constitutional law it was decided unanimously by the league that the main reservation insisted upon by the United States might very well be admitted, and the international court supported and maintained in every important respect, subject to a revision of certain matters pertaining to that court, chiefly matters concerning administration, procedure and the appointments of the members of that august tribunal. But the outstanding question was the question of reservations of the United States, and that question was satisfactorily adjusted.
There is, in the international court as at present constituted, power to give what are

Permanent Court-Optional Clause
known as advisory opinions in regard to certain international difficulties and complications. The court is not asked in every instance to pronounce a final judgment or decree which can be enforced by the League of Nations. It may be asked by the council of the league for what is called an advisory opinion. The United States took the ground and made it one of its express reservations, that where there was asked of the international court any advisory opinion which affected any rights of the United States or which in the opinion of that country affected any of its rights, the United States would not in such case be bound, but might withdraw its adherence from the court altogether. That question seems to have caused considerable difficulty, but a report of a committee of experts was made to the League of Nations, and the report which I read some time ago made by Sir Cecil Hurst seems, in my judgment at all events, to have overcome effectively any objection (there might be to their particular reservation. It has now 'been decreed that the United States Shall have the right to withdraw if it considers that its rights or interests are adversely affected in regard to any matter that is submitted to the international court for advisory opinion and that withdrawal by the United States shall not be considered an act of unwillingness or unfriendliness to any nation which has become a party to the international court.
We are all glad to know that in December last under these reservations the United States accepted the situation and ratified this protocol. It has been ratified by Great Britain. The final signature for which ratification is now asked by this parliament, was given by Canada at Geneva in September last. I believe all right-thinking people, not only in Canada but in all other civilized countries of the world, will agree that this is a step in the right direction and a tremendous advance in regard to the settlement of international disputes over anything -which we have had so far in the history of the world. We all realize that this international tribunal has been set up as the creature of the League of Nations. It is a necessary adjunct, accessory to the League of Nations, a tribunal formed to settle peaceably international disputes and difficulties which might otherwise result in armed conflict.
I know it is the habit in some quarters in this country and in many other countries to criticize rather severely the action and functions of the League of Nations, to disparage its work and influence and to minimize the result of its efforts. I am glad to say for the parliament of Canada that since the inception
of the League of Nations we have supported it most steadfastly and most loyally, and I trust, we may long continue so to do. As I said, in my judgment the League of Nations and the permanent court constitute a tremendous advance over anything which civilization has heretofore enjoyed.
I have had personally little actual experience or contact with that august body, although shortly after the war I had the honour of representing Canada at one of the conferences called under the auspices of the League of Nations in regard to financial matters. I remember attending their meetings and the great interest which I took in the meetings. That conference was held in 1920 at the city of Brussels and we had there representatives from thirty-seven countries. This conference followed almost immediately after the Great war, and what impressed one most at that conference was the ardour and enthusiasm with which the delegates undertook their work. We were in the midst of tremendous wreckage, tremendous financial wreckage. It was said at that time that Europe would never recover financially from the results of the war. This was one of the first conferences held after the war and there was about it a tenseness, an interest, that I have never seen in any other gathering which it has been my privilege to attend. You could see by looking into the faces of the delegates, their earnestness and their desire for the success of what was then more or less an experiment in regard to the League of Nations. The league has now had ten years' operation and while it may not have fulfilled all the desires of all peoples, it has performed an exceedingly useful work in this world during that ten-year period of reconstruction. It may not fulfil all our ideas; it may not fulfil all its own objects; but if it shall succeed in driving from the minds of men the fear of war and removing the burdens of war from the backs of weary multitudes, it will have accomplished for mankind the greatest thing that has been done in this world since Christ was born in Bethlehem.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution moved
by the Prime Minister is one which appeals to me very strongly, chiefly because of the form in which the declaration, signed by Hon. Senator Dandurand at Geneva on September 20, 1929, is expressed. I refer particularly to the reservations therein made, without which it seems to me that it would have been inexpedient indeed that Canada, as a member of the British commonwealth, should have given adherence to the declaration. I remember some years ago reading a declaration which

Permanent Court-Optional Clause
was made by the British Foreign Office on November 27, 1924, to the secretary general of the League of Nations and which seemed to me at the time most commendable in view of the attitude taken by one of the recently formed dominions, the Free State of Ireland. That declaration was:
His Majesty's government has consistently taken the view that neither the covenant of the League of Nations nor any conventions concluded under the auspices of the league are intended to govern the relations inter se of various parts of the British Commonwealth.
In accordance with the spirit of that declaration, which has been accepted by the government of Canada, and will undoubtedly be accepted by parliament in the resolution which is now before the house, Canada has declined to submit to the League of Nations disputes between the government of Canada and the government of any other member of the league which is a member of the British commonwealth of nations, all of which disputes shall hereafter be settled in such a manner as the parties have agreed or shall agree. That reservation meets with my most hearty commendation. I do not know whether the reservation would have been made if the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) had been representing Canada on that occasion, in view of his predilections in favour of sovereignty and independence, but nevertheless it is a reservation which when announced met, I think, with general approval throughout Canada. Only one dominion, the Irish Free State, declined to accept this reservation, and declared that the eompulsoiy jurisdiction of this court, which is external to the British commonwealth, shall be invoked in all disputes between it and any other dominion with which it may have occasion to dispute. I am very-glad to say that every other dominion has declined to follow the lead of the Irish Free State. Even South Africa, although declaring at the time that they rather favoured the attitude of the Irish Free State, declined to follow their example in the express terms of the declaration made on behalf of South Africa on that occasion. I am sure that the people of Canada as a whole are not disposed to agree that a foreign court, even the Permanent Court of International Justice, should have compulsory jurisdiction to decide disputes arising between the dominions inter se.
There is another reservation that I personally commend most heartily, and that is the reservation with respect to disputes with regard to questions which by international law fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada. If I understand that language, and I trust it is broad enough, it
rMr. Cahan.]
is a reservation excluding from the jurisdiction of the Permanent Court of International Justice all disputes between the government of Canada and the government of any other country arising out of domestic matters which are within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, such as tariff, customs and immigration matters. I trust that the language of that reservation is extensive enough to cover all of those matters.
I notice that at the tenth assembly- of the league, at which this document was signed by the Hon. Mr. Dandurand on behalf of the government of Canada, a question was raised by a resolution submitted to the second committee of the league assembly as to whether members of the league were to retain exclusive jurisdiction with respect to immigration into their respective countries. A resolution was presented by a committee of German, Austrian and Italian delegates, and I notice that Mr. Suvich, the Italian delegate, remarked:
The question of circulation of individuals is closely allied to the circulation of commodities, and the two should be treated together. Further, if the Question is only concerned with the circulation of individuals in an economic sphere, the point should be clearly defined in drafting the proposal for reference to the economic committee.
I notice that in commenting upon that a leading British labour member in the Daily Herald of London remarks that common sense demands that all cramped nations shall have room for expansion, and then in a forecast of a world parliament which shall decide these matters emanating from the League of Nations he says:
The incongruity of Australia with a population less than that of London will disappear when these international reforms are fully effected.
He adds:
Then Canada, Siberia, South America and Africa will also accommodate untold millions.
So it was indeed satisfactory I think that this reservation was made by Canada in the fa/ce of a strong and persistent agitation at Geneva to the effect that the League of Nations, through its committees, should have jurisdiction over the economic life of the several members of the league, and should have the right to interfere in such domestic matters as the tariff and immigration. Therefore, when I read the reservations that had been made, I felt in entire agreement with the policy of this government, which I so seldom am able to support.
The attitude of the United States on this question is one of great, almost vital interest to Canada. Our external relations are largely concerned with disputes and differences aris-

Permanent Court-Optional Clause
mg between the two countries. If the United States fails to adopt the optional clause and the compulsory Jurisdiction of the international court, there will be very few questions indeed to which Canada will be a party coming from time to time before that court for decision. The United States acceptance of the international court even under the reservation they have made in case they do not agree with any request for an advisory opinion, simply means that they retain the right to appoint a judge upon the court representing the United States, they retain the right to withdraw at any time if an advisory opinion is asked which they claim affects the rights and interests of the United States, and they also retain the right not to submit any question or dispute or difference which may hereafter arise to that court on which they will appoint a representative. From the discussions which from time to time arise in the Senate and press of the United States it seems to me doubtful indeed whether in any event the Senate of the United States will accept this optional clause conferring compulsory jurisdiction upon the court in disputes to which the United States is a party.
Mr. Elihu Root, who took such an active part in framing the amendments to the constitution of the court in order to secure the adhesion of the United States thereto, has suggested that the acceptance of this compulsory jurisdiction is necessary to put teeth into the court-those are his words, "to put teeth into the court;" while I notice that David Jayne Hill, formerly United States ambassador to Switzerland and subsequently United States ambassador to Germany, I think, who has taken an active interest in this discussion, suggests that the adhesion of the United States to the court without acceptance of its compulsory jurisdiction seems to him to be typical of the gentle art of learning to swim without going near the water, and in one of his erudite discussions of the matter, having so expressed himself, in order that his readers might have no misconception as to what he meant, he quotes the doggerel:
Mother may I go out to swim?
Yes, my darling daughter,
Hang your clothes on a hickory limb
And don't go near the water.
That seems to me to express fully the attitude of the United States with regard to the compulsory jurisdiction of that court, and unless they do accept the optional clause conferring compulsory jurisdiction on the court in matters to which the United States is a party, it will not prove, it seems to me, a very great advantage to us in view of our relations with the United States and of the
difficulties and differences arising between us, which from year to year become more numerous.
So I say that Canada is keenly interested in the final decision of the United States with respect to its acceptance of this compulsory jurisdiction of the court, because, as I stated a moment ago, our international disputes and differences chiefly arise out of our political relations with the United States. Canada is a small nation of nine million people, and we are as keenly conscious of our political rights as any other of the small nations of the world. But we are neighbours to a nation of 120,000,000 people who are proudly conscious at the present time of thedr overwhelming financial and political power, and of their increasing military and naval power. I notice that the United States budget for naval expenditures for-the past year exceeded the naval budgets of England, France and Italy combined, and that the annual expenditure of the United States for naval and military purposes is nearly two-thirds, if I remember correctly, of such expenditures by France, England and Italy combined. Her naval and military expenditures are larger than those of any of these great European nations. Therefore it is a matter of very considerable concern to us as to whether the United States having become a party to the Kellogg pact is now willing, so far as we are concerned, to adjust all disputes arising with us by referring them to the international court.
I have before me a quotation from a recent article written by the ex-president of the United States, who now doubtless feels at liberty to speak more frankly than when he was the executive head of that great republic. In a formal contribution to a Philadelphia journal for April he says:
No sure way has ever been found to prevent war. Opinions may differ as to whether nations with adequate military forces are more likely to enjoy peace than those which neglect their defences. In the last analysis, this is a question of dealing with human nature. Every one knows that if there were no police our cities would be ransacked within twenty-four hours.
Then he adds:
I very strongly suspect that if there were but one nation in the world supplied with an army and a navy, and to make the supposition as strong as possible, if that nation were our own, it would not be long before the other nations had been overrun.
He evidently understands and appreciates public opinion in the country- over which he presided during two terms. He continues:
It seems to me that it is almost a moral certainty that we should find some excuse for taking that action.

I have noticed with alarm the recent efforts of the economic committee of the League of Nations to attempt to frame a common economic policy for all members of the league; I do not believe that those efforts will meet with general approval throughout Canada. Countries which have for more than a century been developing their own industrial institutions and whose increasing .prosperity depends not upon the development of their own internal resources, as We do in this country, but upon the extension of their foreign markets for their manufactured products, are prone to regard less highly industrialized countries such as Canada as being chiefly destined by Providence to produce raw materials for the maintenance of foreign industries, and to receive in compensation therefor foreign manufactured products for domestic consumption in Canada. I noticed at the economic conference, and in the discussions which have taken place from time to time at Geneva in respect thereto, that this doctrine as expressed at the economic conference has become more prevalent in certain countries of Europe which need an outlet for their manufactured products in such countries as Canada. I can understand why my hon. friend should be afraid. I shall state a slight qualification as to my own approval of the reservations as they are, and I shall refer to that in a moment or two. This addition by Canada to the optional clause of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice is I submit the necessary and logical sequence of having taken part in the pact of Paris in 1928. In that pact all the signing nations declared that war would be outlawed, and they would shape their national policies accordingly. That was signed in 1928. When I referred to that pact during the following session of parliament I said that its chief value would consist more particularly in the steps that would follow. If war is to be discarded as a means of solving international difficulties there must be something to take its place, and arbitration, the submission to a world court of conflicts and difficulties between nations, is the necessary and logical method which should replace that of war. It is the organization of peace. War always has been organized; the world is now trying to organize peace, and this must be done not only by words and speeches, but by deeds. This declaration, binding ourselves to the
decisions of the Permanent Court of International Justice in any difficulties which we may have with other nations which are also members of the league or which have adhered to the international court of justice, is the logical step which Should follow. Justice does not mean that nations should be judges in their own cases. They cannot be impartial; there must be a higher court, a more impartial tribunal, and nations as well as individuals must be willing to accept the decisions of that higher tribunal whether or not those conditions are favourable to them. It is sometimes said that a court of this kind may make mistakes, that its decisions may not be always on the side of light. Possibly that may be so, but surely it will be admitted that nations stand a better chance of having right prevail if a tribunal of this kind undertakes the question rather than if a resort is had to arms. Surely bullets and machine guns are poor judges in matters of international law and international difficulties.
I am pleased to say that in this instance Canada has assumed leadership. In 1925, when the Prime Minister, speaking for the government, notified the other nations of the commonwealth, as well as the League of Nations, that we did not consider that we should accept the protocol which had been accepted by the League of Nations at the previous session, he stated at the same time that he was in favour of the arbitration of international difficulties. This stand has been consistently taken by the government of Canada ever since, and at the Imperial conference of 1926, when the question of adhesion by the various parts of the British commonwealth of nations to that optional clause and the international court of justice was being considered, the Canadian delegates stated very clearly that they were in favour of immediate adherence to that optional clause. It is true that at the same time we agreed to postpone our adhesion until the other nations of the commonwealth could further consider the matter and reach a decision, but in a British official white paper issued in December last, the agreement which was inserted in the report of the Imperial conference in 1926 is given as follows:
A general understanding was reached that none of the governments represented at the Imperial conference would take any action in the direction of the acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the permanent court without bringing up the matter for further discussion.
Further, the white paper adds:
Such "further discussion" was begun on the initiative of His Majesty's government in Canada in February, 1929.

We are pleased that all the other nations of the empire have accepted the Canadian viewpoint in this matter, and the fact that the British Empire has signed this optional clause has had a great effect upon the other nations of the world. As a matter of fact, up to July of 1929 this optional clause had been signed by about twelve or fifteen members of the League of Nations. The example of the British commonwealth of nations led many other countries, even while the assembly of the league was meeting, also to accept the optional clause; such important nations as France, Italy, Czechoslovakia and many others have accepted this method of arbitration.
Now I should like to say a word with regard to the reservations which have been made. They are mainly of three classes, as has been stated. The first reservation is when we have agreed to some other method; there are treaties in which there is a clause which mentions how the difficulties in the interpretation of the treaty or the carrying out its provisions will be submitted to arbitration. The second reservation is that it should not apply to the relations of the nations of the British commonwealth, but before speaking further on this reservation I should like to refer to the next one, which excepts all matters of a domestic nature. There can be no difficulty in understanding that any matter which is purely domestic cannot be submitted to the international court of justice by another country.
With reference to the difficulties which may arise between the nations of the commonwealth, my hon. friend said-in a jocular way, I know-he was agreeably surprised that with my well-known ideas about sovereignty and independence, I should accept this reservation. I certainly do accept it. My friend is not using appropriate adjectives when he qualifies my stand in these interdmperial and international matters. Let him stick to the good words " equality of status." That is my position, equality with all the other nations of the empire; that is what I desire to uphold; that is what I stand by, and that is what I am willing to stand by in my public life in Canada. But it is equality.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

They have had a real
civil war in Ireland. Surely the hon. member knows that, and surely there are people in that country who have fought to remain under the British crown. Those people are the leaders in Ireland to-day, and they are directing the destinies of that state. The Irish Free State is one of the jewels of the British commonwealth of nations, and I am always pleased and proud to sit in any conference with delegates from that state.
If those conflicts or difficulties which may arise between the nations of the commonwealth are excluded from settlement by the Permanent Court of International Justice, there must be something to take the place of that court, and this necessity is receiving the attention of public men in Great Britain and other countries of the commonwealth. This matter was raised at the conference which I attended a few months ago, and will be discussed at the next Imperial conference. If difficulties between Australia and Canada should arise, and such may be the case; if difficulties between Canada and the mother country should arise, or between the mother country and Australia, or between Australia and New Zealand, and they cannot be submitted to the Permanent Court of International Justice-we are all parts of a commonwealth, united by a special bond and under one crown and king-then there must be some body or tribunal, whatever it may be called, to which those difficulties should be and must be submitted. I hope no one will be scandalized when I say that the Privy Council as at present constituted could not fill this need; it is not such a tribunal as is the court of international justice. All the member countries of the League of Nations elect representatives to that court, and it is generally recognized that there should be some tribunal to which difficulties between the nations of the commonwealth could be submitted. That body could be of a permanent nature with judges selected by the various nations of the commonwealth, ready to sit at any time when the necessity arose. It has been suggested that it be merely an institution which would be available when the need arose, every nation in advance having submitted a list of names forming a panel out of which a certain number should be selected for every special case that might come up. This is a very important subject which ought to receive consideration everywhere, and I am sure that on this subject, as
on all other matters, the common sense of the various nations of the commonwealth will see to it that a proper solution is found. I apologize for having spoken as long as I have as it was not my intention to do so.
Let me repeat in conclusion that I am pleased with the work done by Canada in those international matters in the League of Nations, the Peace pact and the international court of justice. My hon. friend regretted that the United States of America has not yet accepted the optional clause of the statute of the Permanent Court of International Justice. We must be pleased indeed that so much progress has been made that they have joined the international court of justice. The mere acceptance by the United State of this tribunal, which is really the creation of the League of Nations, is indeed a great achievement.

It is agreed that they
accept the court. The rest will, I hope, come. From the beginning we have not waited for the United States; we were there before they were there. Mr. Speaker, I heartily approve the steps taken by the government in this regard. It is in conformity, first, with the declarations of their own members and, more broadly, I think it is in conformity with the tendencies of the Canadian people for many years past. In several past instances, which I am not going to discuss because it would take too much time, Canada has indicated that she relies upon the principle of arbitration to settle most of her difficulties with the United States, to which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has alluded especially. I am glad the hon. member brought that point up, because undoubtedly, as he says-
' and this should be stated oftener-practically the whole of our international situation is governed by our neighbourhood to the United States. It is preposterous to imagine that Canada could, in international affairs, assume an attitude in violent contradistinction to that taken by her only neighbour on the continent of North America. It is mere delusion to imagine that we could stand up against the United States on any international issue, either as an isolated nation or even counting upon the theoretical support of the British Empire.
My eyes were first opened with respect to this situation by a man whose authority, or at least whose devotion to British institutions, will not be questioned in the house. I refer to the late Sir Charles Tupper. When leading the opposition in parliament from 1896 to 1900, he stated, with regard to the Alaskan boundary affair, that the result of his many years' experience in dealing, either in his capacity as High Commissioner for Canada in London or as a member of the Canadian government, with affairs in which Canada on the one hand and the United States on the other were interested, the unfailing attitude of the British government was to side with the United States and against Canada. This he explained, and history explains it still more fully, without the necessity of resorting to such denunciations of British policy as at times have been resorted to, even by Toronto judges writing books to denounce British diplomacy from beginning to end. In our state of colonial infancy, with that disposition of mind of the spoiled child,

always expecting that his father will stand by him in all his impertinences, we imagined that every time we had matters at issue with the United States, the power of England would be available if necessary to sustain a war in our defence. But the British statesmen who are responsible for the affairs, the safety, the trade and commerce, and the foreign relations of the United Kingdom and of the hundreds of lands which come under the jurisdiction of the British government and involve its national and international responsibility-British statesmen cannot take that one-sided view. Soon after the secession of the American colonies to the south of us, they realized that under any circumstances war between the United States and Great Britain was preposterous; they felt that, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has said generally,-but more especially is it applicable to this case-a war between the United States and Great Britain could not settle anything, and still less as regards Canada. Therefore, I have always held the view, and stated it in public, that even in those instances where we felt rather irritated at the attitude of the British government, the best service which the British could render us was precisely to avoid war with the United States.
Putting the question on more general ground, it is a significant feature of this movement in favour of arbitration that in Europe it has first been taken up and propounded-[DOT] it is now on the point of becoming slowly but surely the basis of international relations -by small nations; and it has been first taken up on the continent of North America by the weaker of the two nations which practically divide between themselves that continent. The acceptance of the principle of arbitration is the only safeguard of small nations as against the ambitions, the greediness, or simply the instinctive power of domination of large nations. Therefore, in agreeing to this further measure of arbitration, the government has rendered a service not only to Canada but to all small nations within or without the British association of nations -yes, a service to all, and the most effective service that they can render to international justice and international peace.
Of course, there is still plenty of scepticism. People say: It is all very well to declare in favour of arbitration, to pass resolutions, to have protocols voted at Geneva, and to have the adhesions of parliaments; but what will that amount to when a great nation declares war? They quote as instances the attitude of Italy towards Greece, or of Poland towards Lithuania, and the failure of the League of Nations to prevent those acts of international brigandage. Well, of course, things of

Permanent Court-Optional Clause
that kind will happen, as they have happened in the past. Before tribunals of justice were established in the various countries, before savages, in the formation of nations, agreed to resort to some form of adjudication to settle individual quarrels, it took some time. For quite a while blood was still shed and heads were knocked off before the principle of justice as applied to individuals prevailed over the practices of barbarism; and it will undoubtedly take some time before the so-called Christian but largely dechristianized nations accept and adopt the principle of arbitration, instead of resorting to war if they feel that they are powerful enough to overcome their opponent. Of course, it will take time; butt is that a reason why the principle should not be propounded? Is that a reason why small nations especially, that are not in a position to rely upon force of arms, and who should not, if their pretensions to higher civilization are true, rely on the force of arms even if they had the power in their hands- is that a reason, because it takes time, or because you may still quote this act or that act of this or that government against the acceptance of the principle, that we should not preach it?
Therefore I think it is in conformity with the better spirit of the age and with the true interests of Canada thait we should uphold by all means that principle. It is especially true having regard to our relations with the United States. I remember one day at a meeting somewhere in the state of New York where representatives of various European and American nations had gathered together to discuss international affairs, an American gentleman-I think he was a member of the Department of State, but it does not matter -a highly cultured man, quoted as an instance of the possibility of gradually bringing the American nation to take a broader and more generous view of international affairs, the difference between the United States of America and the republic of Colombia with regard to the Panama canal. Of course, all fair-minded Americans admit now that that was an act of high-handed piracy, if I may use the word, on the part of the United States government. The delegates of that small republic, Colombia, went to Europe, or to the other South American countries and endeavoured to raise a feeling of animosity against the United States. Naturally it did not materialize. Then, one or [DOT] two or a few of them got the idea that if they came right straight to the United States and appealed to their sense of justice and generosity, they might obtain a different result, and they did obtain a different result; for after a few years
the congress of the United States passed legislation to compensate the Republic of Colombia for the dispossession to which they had been subjected by the government of the United States in that matter. In his discussion of that situation, the speaker concluded with this thought, that the spirit of justice is inherent in the mind of the average American just as it is in the mind of all normal human beings; but in international matters they had been so long accustomed to consider themselves as being so completely masters of the continent in which they live that they had never realized that there was such a thing as equality of rights between them and other nations. But now, and since the war especially,-perhaps this is one of the redeeming features of that horrible slaughter, that fit of human craziness which lasted four years- the Americans, and the British, and the French, and the Germans, all peoples that have made great sacrifices in the war, realize that no one nation in the long run is capable of ruling the world, and that therefore as between all nations, weak and strong, populous or less numerous, there must be found some means of deciding issues according to justice, according to equity, according to the facts as presented before an impartial body. That feeling, I sincerely believe, is growing in the United States, and we should do everything we can to encourage it because we are more interested than any other nation on earth in going, so to speak, in advance of that evolution of thought in the United States.
Now, let us consider the case of the nations composing what the Minister of Justice, after others, calls the commonwealth of nations. Of course, I believe, with others also, that the word "commonwealth" is a misnomer, just as the word empire was a misnomer; and in this case it is not my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) who suggests to me the idea; it was expressed some twenty years ago by such a pillar of the British Empire as Lord Milner. The word "commonwealth", as applied to the aggregation of the various nations associated under the British crown, is a greater absurdity even than the word "empire". Nevertheless, words are not much. The fact remains that at present there are several nations that acknowledge as their sovereign the sovereign who presides nominally over the affairs of England. It is a new form of personal union such as existed before the act of 1707 between Scotland and England, and which, in later years, existed between England and Hanover when the elector of Hanover was at the same time king of Great Britain. It is a new form of personal union under which -not altogether in fact yet, but in principle,

as proposed by the Imperial conference of 1926, and as admitted even now by such upholders of the old imperial system as Professor Keith, for example-the advisers of the crown in Canada are absolutely independent of the advisers of the crown in Great Britain, and the king or his representative in Canada, or Australia, or South Africa, has to govern by the sole advice of his ministers in each country.
Well, if this is true-and it ought to be made truer and truer every day-then surely there must also be found some means of arbitrating between those nations, equal in right, equal in international status, as has been found necessary between the whole of those associated British nations and foreign countries. In that respect I am glad to hear the Minister of Justice state that at the next Imperial conference this idea of arbitration as between the various British self-governing nations will be advanced a step further. In this also the present or any other government will have the full support of all true Canadians; because even should there be a change of government-

-there is one thing
sure, and it is this, that no government of the future, whether it is called Tory, Progressive or by any other name, will be powerful enough to stem the tide of self dignity and self conscience of the growing Canadian nation.
How illuminating are the reflections that were made last year at the Imperial conference, or later by commentators on the work of that conference, about the application of the Colonial Laws Validity Act. It is considered now as the last outstanding obstacle against the true operation of self-government in the various dominions. When that piece of legislation was passed, only sixty-five years ago, it was not only considered, but was in fact a long step in advance of the principle of self-government as then understood; and to-day the sentiment, and the facts, are just as much in advance of what sixty-five years ago was an advance on what had happened previously. Which shows once more, sir, that under all forms of government the true grandeur of British institutions is that there is no finality in their growth and their development.
That is the one feature which holds together peoples of different racial origin, peoples who in periods of their history have suffered at

the hands of British representatives, who have been forced to resist for years and for centuries the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by some representatives of the British crown and of the British race. It is the one feature which, in spite of all those past difficulties and straggles, binds us to British institutions, because we find in them a perpetual spirit of growth, of progress, of expansion, which makes them bigger than the British races, bigger than the little islands of northern Europe, which make them big enough for all right-thinking nations who want to exercise their rights as British citizens, as well as discharge their duties as such, to live under those institutions with respect for themselves and for others. That perhaps explains the fact that the Minister of Justice endeavoured to make my good friend from Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) understand as regards Ireland.
As the most ancient and genuine representative of Sinn Fein Ireland in this house, I am bound to take some exception to what the Minister of Justice said. The very able gentlemen who rule the Free State of Ireland to-day did not fight to maintain the authority of the British king in Ireland. No. You could not expect them to do that. The Minister of Justice has spoken of the impatience of the Irish. Well, they had to wait six centuries before they could hold their own. It is not for the British king that they have fought, but for maintenance of the treaty with Great Britain. As the representatives of a nation impoverished, ruined, cut in half by starvation, persecution and all forms of foreign domination for centuries, they decided to enter into a treaty with the nation that dominated them, that persecuted them for centuries, but a nation which at last opened its eyes, a nation whose slow-growing process of respect for others has brought it at last to forget its ambitions of the past. The Irish responded generously and loyally to the offer of truce, to the offer of peace, to the offer of alliance on the part of the British government. They accepted the offer, and now look upon the king of England, not as their king because he is king in England, but as their king as he is the king of Canada, the king of Australia, the king of South Africa,- a country also composed of a brave race which fought for many years against British domination, but which is as proud as the Irish and the French-Canadians to be in the fraternity of British nations, not, however, in any subservient state and not looking upon the king as the emblem of foreign domination, but on the contrary, as the head of their own institutions. It is not on account of loyalty to the

St. Lawrence Waterway
king of England-there is no reason for Ireland to be loyal to the king of England-but it is on account of loyalty to Ireland, to their own plighted word, that the Irish government through a cruel civil war have struggled to make their word good, and fought to make the principle of equality acknowledged by their own people as they have succeeded after six centuries of resistance to arrogant domination in having the dominating partner acknowledge also that spirit of equality. And it is no wonder, sir, if the representatives of the Irish Free State have also been pioneers in advocating the principle of arbitration, and if they are a little more concerned than we are in making it clear that they are not under even the most indirect obligation to England or any other part of the empire.
There, sir, is another example of the true spirit of conciliation. There is another example of what the true spirit of partnership and arbitration can accomplish. Who would have thought twenty years ago that the people of England and the people of Ireland could have come to such terms as those upon which the two nations live together at the present time? I will not say they live in amity, we cannot expect that so soon; but they live in loyal partnership. They are loyal first to themselves; they are loyal to the people with whom they have formed those terms of partnership and they have formulated a principle and a practice of arbitration which stands as an object lesson given to the various associated nations of the so-called British commonwealth and to the rest of the world.
I hope to live long enough to see this government or any other government representing the people of Canada, when differences arise between us and any other nation of the world, whether they be black, yellow or white, or with our relatives who call themselves British, stand by the principle of arbitration and conciliation, and not by the brutal practice of war and bloodshed.

On section 1-Power to make regulations.

As some of the hon. members wish to know the object of this bill, may I say that section 1 authorizes the governor in council to make regulations governing the traffic on parks, boulevards and roads owned by the federal government, over which there exists no public right of way.
But you do not say "federal government." You do not limit it to that.
We say "which are situate on the property of His Majesty."

Can you not limit it to
His Majesty's property in the right of the Dominion government?

That is the intention, I
may say. The bill says "situate on the property of His Majesty."
I think in this case that would be implied to mean on land over which the federal government have jurisdiction.

I would say to my hon. friend, as has been suggested by the hon. member for South Wellington, that this government would not be able to legislate with regard to property of His Majesty which is not owned in the right of the Dominion.
I dislike these implications; when you want to say a thing, say it. The English language is plain enough to say anything which you intend.

I think it covers what is intended and I may say to my hon. friend that the Department of Justice is of the opinion that that is the case. This act was submitted to the Department of Justice and I am advised by the officers of that department that that is what it covers, and nothing else.

While the minister is on this section may I ask whether this government has any jurisdiction at all with regard to Wellington street, as it adjoins the parliament buildings. There are traffic regulations in force there under the control of the city of Ottawa; have we any authority or control over that traffic? Day after day I cross that street, and I notice that those lights are disregarded almost entirely. Our Dominion officers are standing at the gates, and they could easily take the numbers of these machines which violate the law. Have we any right to enforce the traffic laws on Wellington street?

My information is that that is under the jurisdiction of the police officers of the city of Ottawa.

Could we make an arrangement with the city whereby the Dominion officers could lay these complaints? There are no police officers of the city of Ottawa on this street. I think the matter to which I am about to refer should be brought to the attention of the minister. Instances have occurred where fire insurance companies have issued policies providing insurance coverage on a building designated in the policy, and the people concerned have subsequently discovered that they have been paying a premium upon a building which is non-existent. We have had a sad occurrence in my section of the country, where many of the people suffered to the extent of an aggregate of over half a million dollars through the fraudulent undertakings of a trusted lawyer. This lawyer agreed to obtain mortgages on houses in the vicinity of Toronto, and the people trusted in his knowledge that these buildings existed. The mortgages came along with fire and wind insurance policies attached thereto. In the case of my own family, out of sixteen such mortgages with sixteen fire insurance policies attached to cover sixteen houses, there were only six buildings of any kind actually existent. I contend that the fire insurance companies were a party to the fraud. Each of the mortgages we received had a fire insurance policy attached, signed by a reputable fire insurance company, which stated that they were insuring a house of a certain kind, on a certain lot, built in a certain manner, when in fact there was no house at all. This fraud took place in the Listowel and Stratford section, and was extended into my constituency. Let me emphasize the fact that the fire insurance companies placed policies upon buildings which did not exist, although they described in the policy as the nature and construction of the buildings alleged to be insured; thus they have been assisting in the carrying out of fraudulent transactions which have resulted in the people in my district being robbed of nearly three-quarters of a million dollars. I would like to see the act amended to provide that when a fire insurance company issues a policy which is a contract of insurance upon a building they shall inspect the property or otherwise make sure that the building in respect of which the policy is written really exists. Fire insurance companies are collecting hundreds of dollars of insurance premiums on buildings that do not exist-merely on vacant lots. It would be much cheaper to buy an asbestos blanket. I do not know whether this is the proper time to make the suggestion, but if fire insurance companies are coming to parliament for additional assistance I would ask the minister to see to it that the people are protected from being swindled by fire insurance companies through the issuing of fire insurance policies upon buildings which do not exist.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot say offhand
whether or not the law as it now exists would provide a means of dealing with cases such as that to which my hon. friend refers.
I hope I did not gather from him what at one stage I thought I did, namely, that this form of fire insurance fraud had amounted to three-quarters of a million dollars.

In operation through
Listowel alone it is about half a million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On buildings that do not exist?

Insurance on fictitious
mortgages.

But in each case a fire
insurance policy was given and the people took it. The insurance company said they were insuring a building which naturally would be presumed to exist, but the building was not there; it was merely a vacant lot.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall be glad to bring the matter to the attention of the superintendent of insurance with a view to having the state of the law in that regard looked into and the superintendent of insurance may be able to take some action to deal with that sort of thing. I hesitate to suggest to my hon. friend1 that a man who takes a mortgage on property ought to determine for himself whether or not the property exists. A little responsibility rests upon him.

I grant that, but when
you receive a fire insurance policy stating that in consideration of a certain premium the company is insuring a building which is described in the policy, there is in that, one would think, some measure of security.

I think the situation is
worse than the hon. member for North Huron has just indicated, because I believe that in respect to each section of the country the underwriters have plans on which each building within that territory is shown. If an insurance company had such plans covering the
Insurance Act

section of the country in which my hon. friend lives, the situation is much worse, because if no buildings were shown on the plan I do not see how the company could issue insurance on buildings that do not exist.

That is the case, only in towns and cities. While I realize that this matter is not really apropos of the subject under discussion, if the minister is going to bring it to the attention of the superintendent of insurance it might be well for me to bring to his notice another feature which I have in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend
continues, will he permit me to say I cannot guarantee that the companies in question are Dominion companies? As my hon. friend doubtless knows, companies incorporated by the provinces do not come within the jurisdiction of the Dominion. I shall, however, be glad to bring the incident to the attention of the superintendent of insurance in order that inquiry may be made with a view to protecting the public so far as it is reasonably possible to do so.

What I shall refer to will be
under the jurisdiction of the Dominion. It is a common thing for a company to place insurance on buildings valued at $1,000, $1,500 or $2,000, the premium being paid for a number of years, and then when there is a loss the value is disputed. Something should be done in that regard. I have at the present time a case pending in that category. The insurance companies have agents; the agents inspect the risks, and I cannot see that it is in order for an insurance company which accepts a certain premium after the inspection of the property by one of its own agents, to be permitted to dispute the loss in the case of total destruction of the property so insured. That sort of thing is done right along, and I suggest to the minister that it is a matter well worthy of consideration. I know how these things very often happen. Perhaps you go into a local agent to place a policy; you are in a hurry to get it; the application is taken, and the agent perhaps does not know the property at the time, but he has an opportunity of seeing it shortly afterwards. He should see it andi if he thinks the value placed on it is too high he should either insist upon the amount of the policy being reduced to a fair value or decline to take the risk. I ask the minister to request the superintendent of insurance to consider that feature seriously.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall have it looked
nto.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister another matter that arises out of a recent decision in the courts of Ontario under circumstances somewhat as follows: a farmer goes to an insurance agent and asks him to fill out the application form for him. The insurance agent, with full knowledge of the conditions, makes an inaccurate or perhaps an absolutely untrue statement as an answer to one of the questions in the application. The insurance goes through on the basis of that application.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I presume that untrue
statement is signed by the applicant.

Signed by the applicant, sometimes by the insurance agent signing the applicant's name, with his authority; but the application is filled out by the insurance agent, although, of course, as the minister says, for practical purposes it bears the signature of the applicant. Nevertheless the fact is that the misstatement made by the agent of the company in full knowledge of the facts, and the decision of the court is that that is held to be the statement of the applicant. The insurance company assumes no responsibility and escapes all liability arising from the wrongful act of its own agent, because he is technically held to be the agent of the applicant. These are matters that are causing injustice and working very grave hardship, especially in the particular case I have in mind. It seems to me that this parliament, so far as lies within its power, should insert in the Insurance Act a provision that when an agent of the company acts in the manner I have indicated, the company should be estopped from denying responsibility for the act of the man who is really its own agent for that purpose.
