speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Railways) :
speechtext: The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) inquired yesterday when the annual report of the Canadian National Steamships would be tabled. I was out of the house when this question was asked, but I would inform my hon. friend that it is expected that the report will be tabled shortly after the recess.

Hon. PETER HEENAN (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 49, respecting fair wages and an eight hour day for labour employed on public works of the Dominion of Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when this bill was introduced, some hon. members asked that an explanation be given, and I promised to give it when the bill was next before the house. A reference to the bill will disclose that it is to apply to contractors and subcontractors on Dominion government work, subh as construction, remodelling, repair or demolition of any work. It also applies to the workmen employed by the government on similar undertakings, to those workmen generally known as day labourers. The bill provides for the payment of wages which are current in the district, but there is an added provision which differs from our present fair wage policy, that in all cases the wages must be fair and reasonable. An eight hour day is provided for on all work, except special cases or emergencies. A few weeks ago I had the honour of tabling an order in council which provided for an eight hour day for all employees of the Dominion government, and with the addition of this bill the principle of the eight hour day will be applicable to the entire Dominion public service. Representations have been made that the provisions of this bill would apply to manufacturers, but I desire to make it clear that this bill is not intended to be applied to that class. When the bill is in committee I propose to move an amendment to add a subsection which will make it perfectly clear that manufacturers are not to be included.
142S
Fair Wages and Hours
Would the minister read that amendment now?

No, I cannot. In order to administer a bill of this character, it will be necessary to hare rules and regulations, and this bill gives the governor in council authority in that regard. Regulations may be made for the following:
(a)	The method of determining what are current or fair and reasonable wages and the preparation and use of schedules of rates relating thereto,
(b)	rates of wages for overtime,
(c)	classifications of employment or work,
(d)	the publication and posting of wage schedules.
(e)	payment of wages to employees in case of default by the contractor or other party charged with such payment and recovery thereof from such contractor or other party,
(f)	the keeping of proper books and records and the examination of the same by government officers,
(g)	persons who may be employed on works referred to in this act,
(h)	the subletting of contracts,
(i)	the penalties to be imposed for breaches of the provisions of this act or regulations made hereunder,
(j)	generally for the due enforcement of the provisions of the act and regulations.
Under our present fair wage policy, regulations have to be made from time to time in order to cope with the different problems which may arise. It has been said that this bill is limited in its scope because of the fact that it is confined to building and construction, but otherwise I would point out that it in no way replaces the present fair wage regulations as provided by order in council. It is a distinct step forward in our fair wage policy, and so far as I can learn this is the first bill of its kind in the history of Canada. The question has been asked, why the fair wage policy as applied to water power development and railroads is not embodied in this bill. I would point out that the policy regarding the development of water powers is contained in regulations under another act. Matters pertaining to railways are covered under section 244 of the Railway Act. The manufacture of supplies, material, equipment and so on, is now taken care of under our present order in council. I am mentioning this to the house so that it will not be thought that railroads, manufacturers and enterprises of that sort are neglected. The bill applies to the construction, demolition, repair and so on of public buildings and the government thinks it a good thing to start its fair wage legislation in a not too advanced manner. This is all the information that I have at the present time, but I may have to reply to some comment later on.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, undoubtedly the government is to be congratulated upon having brought in a bill of this character. It might be very easy, if somewhat ungracious, for us to say that it is long overdue. The government has been committed to the eight-hour day ever since the signing of the Peace treaty, and though to a considerable extent the eight-hour day on government works has been provided for by orders in council or in other ways, there seems to be no reason why it should not have been made statutory. I am glad, indeed, that definite legislation of this character has been introduced. The minister said that this was a distinct step in advance. That is true. The only criticism that we in this corner can offer is that, as the minister has recognized, it is somewhat limited in scope. I am not sure that work on harbours, for example, is provided for at the present time. We have a number of harbour boards that are more or less public in character. Certainly they are subsidized, or are given large loans by the Dominion government, in some instances the interest not being paid very promptly, so that I think they may be regarded as being in reality federal works. I would like to have seen harbour boards included in a matter of this kind.
Although it may be true that the railways and water-powers are provided for by the orders in council, it is not very clear, since we are departing from the order in council arrangement and substituting therefor statutory regulations, why the latter ought not to apply to the Canadian National Railways or to other contracts.
The most serious deficiency, however, in this legislation seems to me to be the continued use of the word "current" in relation to wages. I mentioned that when the bill was first introduced. I should much prefer to have seen some such phrase as "standard wage" or "minimum standard wage." In the draft bill which was presented by the executive council of the Trades and Labour Congress to the government, I notice that there is a definition of "standard" which I would commend to the attention of the minister:
"Standard," when used with respect to hours of work on any undertaking, means a number of hours in each period of twenty-four hours not greater than the number of hours commonly worked by persons in like occupations in the locality in which such undertaking is carried out, and when used with respect to rates of pay for work on any undertaking, means rates of pay for ordinary and overtime work at least equal either to those which are recognized as payable to persons in like occupations by both employers and trade unions in the locality aforesaid, or if no such rates of pay are so

Fair TTcijes and Hours
recognized, then to those paid to persons in like occupations by the majority of substantial and established employers of persons in like occupations in such locality, provided that, if in such locality the conditions are such that the comparisons aforesaid cannot be made, then the bases for comparison shall be the hours of labour and rates of pay recognized or commonly worked or paid as aforesaid by or to persons in like occupations at the places from which the workmen employed on such undertaking are drawn; and provided also that rates of pay shall in all eases be such as are fair and reasonable.
There are special cases which I might cite as illustrating the need of some definition of this character. In connection with some of the hydro developments just outside of my own city we had an example of this where the rates of pay in the locality did not mean anything. The construction work was practically in the wilderness. The men themselves had mostly to be drawn from Winnipeg and there was no provision for the payment of wages such as were prevalent in that city. It would seem to me that if the minister could be induced to incorporate some such phrase as this with some such definition as this, he would make the bill a great deal more satisfactory. Of course I have very little doubt that the minister himself will interpret the act as generously as possible, but since we are getting away from mere orders in council and since I do not think that matters of this kind should be left to the discretion even of the most sympathetic minister, I should like to have seen this interpretation incorporated in the legislation itself.

Does the hon. member
not think that is sufficiently provided for in subsection (a) of section three where it is provided:
Provided that wages shall in all cases be such as are fair and reasonable.

That is left, as I
am suggesting, to the discretion of the minister. The phrase "fair and reasonable" is a fair and reasonable sort of phrase, but I should like to have something a little more definite than that. There is a weakness in regard to definiteness.
Mr. CHAPLI'N:	How would a contractor
view that phrase?
There is the difficulty.
Of course there is.

The contractor
thinks in terms of his profits as to what is fair and reasonable, and what can be paid by other contractors in other parts of the country. The wage earner sees the matter
in a very different light. The Minister of Labour might have difficulty sometimes in finding a way of harmonizing the two ideas, that of the contractor and that of the wage earner.
If the hon. member would not like to leave that matter in the hands of the minister, would a contractor likely want it left there?

I recognize the difficulty and that is why I suggest that it would be better if we had something definite. Undoubtedly, however, this is a move in the right direction. The minister, if I heard him correctly, took the ground that he did not wish to be too much in advance. Perhaps that is a safe policy to pursue, but I think the government should be at least a model employer and should be just a little in advance of the ordinary ideals and practices that may exist in the community round about. So I think there is not much danger in going a few steps ahead of the ordinary practice round about us when the government is so definitely committed by treaty to the underlying principle. However, I shall heartily support the legislation, hoping that the minister may be able to see his way to modify the bill a little along the lines that I have suggested.

May I ask if the minister will reconsider the decision that he gave a moment ago not to put the house into possession of information as to the details of the amendment that he says he will introduce in committee? It might be of the very greatest importance. I think we ought to have it before us. It has evidently been definitely decided upon, and I think it is only right that the house should know the details of the proposed amendment before the vote on the second reading is taken.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) is entirely right in making that request. The question may arise whether the amendment is in order if it conflicts with the general principle of the bill. I think the amendment should be given to the house before the hon. minister moves the second reading of the bill.
The reason I did not give it is that in my innocence I did not think that this was the proper place to discuss the amendment.
If it affects the principle of the bill we have a right to know it.

It was handed to me only a few moments ago, so perhaps my hon. friends will not be too critical as to the precise wording. What I intended to do was to make it
Fair Wages and Hours

perfectly clear that the bill should not apply to industries where the manufacturer was making supplies or equipment for use in the work contemplated. The substance of the amendment is this:
The provisions of this section shall not apply to persons employed in the fabrication or the manufacture of materials, supplies or equipment for use in the "work contemplated where such fabrication or manufacture is carried on in any established plant of factory other than a plant or factory established for the purpose of the work contemplated.
May I ask whether the present order in council covers the workmen in such factories?
Yes.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre):
speechtext: I am very strongly in favour of the principle underlying this bill. I have previously urged in this house that the Dominion government should set itself up as a model employer of labour in so far as it is possible for it to do so. I am very glad indeed to see the government implement its obligations in the matter of a fair wage and the eight-hour day in so far as it lies within the power of this parliament to enact such a measure. It seems to me that the rights of the workmen are amply safeguarded by subsection (a) of section 3 of the bill, which provides that wages shall in all cases be such as are fair and reasonable. I agree, of course, that the words "fair and reasonable" are not definite. They cannot in the nature of things be absolutely definite. But the words "fair and reasonable" have a well-known meaning in law. The question is one of fact in all cases, depending on all the circumstances of the case. The subsection will, I think, accomplish the purpose that it is desired to serve. I for one would like to take this opportunity of commending the Minister of Labour for his support of this measure. The bill is approved in principle' by organized labour throughout this country, and I believe that it will serve a very useful purpose. I am thoroughly in ac-:ord with the underlying principle of the bill.
Will the terms of this bill apply to existing contracts?
No, to future contracts.

I
must at the outset congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) upon bringing down this bill, not only on behalf of myself, but on behalf of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, from whose president I have received a letter in which he urges support of this bill and that congratulations be extended to the government for bringing it down.

A year or so ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was asked about the enforcement of the eight-hour day, and he replied that it was purely a provincial matter. We are glad to note that so far as this government and its employees are concerned, the government are showing their sincerity by putting into effect the recommendations of the League of Nations and of the conference held at Washington some years ago.
A few days ago my friends to my right, from Nova Scotia, were berating the Minister of Labour because of the low wages paid to some of the government employees in that province, and they made the statement, if I remember aright, that this government should lead the way and show how things should be done, be a little in advance of other employers. I hope, therefore, now that this measure has been brought down, that our friends from Nova Scotia will heartily support it because it is a distinct advance so far as labour is concerned. It gives labour the eight-hour day and seeks to provide a fair wage clause. Where the words "prevailing rate" were used in the old regulation, the words used in this bill are "fair and reasonable," and what is fair and reasonable is to be determined by the Minister of Labour, and not by any twenty-five cents an hour rate, which has been so much complained' of by our friends from Nova Scotia. I congratulate the minister upon that. Personally I would like to have seen the bill go a little further, but because of the objections that have been raised by contractors and others the minister is perhaps a little timid about going too far. I think, however, we could safely make statutory enactments covering specific works. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was rather afraid that the employees of the harbour commissions to which loans are made by this government would not be included in this bill. They may or may not be. I remember, however, that last year when the harbour commissions were under consideration and their estimates being voted, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) assured me that a fair wage clause such as is provided in this bill would be put in all the contracts for the construction of harbour works, under the loans of this government. I have a copy of the message that he sent to me. He said: The contractor pledges himself to adhere to the government fair wage schedule in force in Montreal during the different periods of construct ion.
The minister sent to me personally a copy of the fair wage clause that is used in contracts for harbour commission work that is being done under government loan. I do not

Fair Wages and Hours
think it would hurt this bill at all if it included a statutory enactment covering the harbour commissions and other works that are being done under government loan. The fair wage clause should be made applicable to all such works.
As regards hydro-electric, undertakings it is quite true that the minister by order in council may insist on the fair wage clause in connection with the issue of the license. I hope the house will observe the principle that has been laid down. For instance, in the hydro-electric licence to the Calgary company, the fair wage clause was inserted. The federal government has not a dollar invested in that enterprise; it has simply granted a licence to a company to do certain work; thereby, in my opinion, the principle has been laid down that in such licences the fair wage clause may be incorporated. In view of this, I would suggest that in the near future this precedent should be followed with respect to all licences granted by the government. Again I congratulate the minister on the bill and I will support it.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) and the government must be congratulated for having introduced in the house a measure of such far reaching importance. This bill aims at establishing, in connection with government contracts, an eight hour day, with fair and equitable wages for the labourer. The government is equally entitled to our congratulations for endeavouring to put through this measure because it gives an example to the people of this country which should be followed by all those who employ workers in their manufactures or commercial pursuit. The workman is the most important factor in industry. By his work, he contributes the most to production, and consequently gives to the manufacturer the greatest possible returns. This factor must not be overlooked, and special considerations must be given to it when the times comes to remunerate the worker for his labours.
As the representative of a riding the major part being artisans, I am in favour of this bill and I again congratulate the government for having had the courage of introducing, so worthy a measure as the one actually under consideration. I think the working classes will be pleased and happy to find in this house friends ready to acknowledge that human capital must receive a just and equitable treatment, which will give to the workers, not only the opportunity of providing for the needs of their family, but also of saving a little money for their old age.
Such a measure should receive the unanimous support of the house, and I have every reason to believe that the people of this country will unanimously support the government in order to prove their appreciation for this piece of legislation.

Heretofore
when tenders were called for public works it was quite possible for the contracting firms to estimate the wages that would be paid because they were the wages current in the locality at the time. Now we have a different method, it being provided by section 5, subsection (a) that the governor in council may make regulations with regard to:
(a) the method of determining what are current or fair and reasonable wages and the preparation and use of schedules of rates relating thereto.
This being the case, is it the intention of the minister when tenders are being called for to furnish the prospective contractors with a schedule of the rates of wages that will apply on the work so that those tendering will be able to make an intelligent estimate?

That is the intention, to
provide a schedule of wages with the specifications.
And all the conditions with regard to extras, and so on?
Yes.

I
observe that section 3, subsection (a) provides for the payment of such wages "as are generally accepted as current from time to time." Does this mean that the wages may be changed during the progress of the work?
That is the system at the present time. If the current wages in the locality are changed, we have a right to increase in proportion the wages to be paid by the contractor.

Clause (h) of section 5 provides that the governor in council may make regulations with regard to the subletting of contracts. How will that work out? I would point out that some question has been raised by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with regard to a definite standard of wages being set. In the opinion of the Trades and Labour Congress the words:
provided that wages shall in all cases be such as are fair and reasonable.
do not give the minister sufficient control over the rates of wages which may be paid. I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre when he says that
Fair Wages and Hours

the door is left wide open for some interpretation that may not suit the working men to say the least. Again, if there is such a standard or current rate of wages as was said the other day to prevail in Nova Scotia, is it proposed under this proviso that the department may increase that current rate to something that it thinks is fair and reasonable?
Surely that is contemplated as possible.

If my hon. friend will allow
the minister to answer I hope I shall get the information that I desire. The next question I should like to put to the minister is as to whether this section will be inserted in each contract. I see some difficulties in prospect if it is just left as a statutory enactment. I know the minister wants to make the legislation effective, and I think he should consider the advisability of inserting this provision as a term of each contract. I thoroughly approve of the principle of this bill, but like my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, I regret it has been so long delayed. It is welcome legislation in regard to hours of labour and rates of wages.
I can hope only that the government will do what we on this side of the house have been urging it to do for some time. Irrespective of parties, we have been urging the government to consider the fact that within the scope of its own jurisdiction, and in regard to its own employees, the government is paying far from a living wage to great numbers of workers. There are men who are receiving SSO a month and upwards; some of those men have families and are trying to exist on that wage. It seems to me that the Dominion government should take into consideration this session, as it has been urged to do in previous sessions, the question whether it should continue to pay a wage as low as $80 a month to men who are capable of doing the work to which they are assigned. We will later have the opportunity to deal with this question. I will be pleased if the minister will answer my questions, so that the matter may be clarified in my mind. I approve of the general principle of the bill and I welcome it.

If my hon. friend does
not mind I would prefer to wait until we reach the committee stage; at that time I will be pleased to answer his questions clause by clause.
That is a fair answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Before second reading is given
to this bill I wish to join issue with those
(Mr. Geary.]
who have so heartily congratulated the government upon taking action in this matter. My colleague from East Calgary (Mr. Ads-head) seems to think that the fact the government is now taking action is a cause for great jubilation and congratulation. As I read the records of international gatherings this measure is about ten years past due; that is all. At a great international conference at which employers and employees were represented steps were taken to give effect to the provisions of the treaty of Versailles. To put it shortly, that treaty made provision for an eight-hour day, and the Dominion of Canada became a party to it. The constitutional jurisdiction of the Dominion to give effect to such hours of employment was questioned, and it was contended that the provinces alone could deal with the question of an eight-hour day. It will no doubt be within the memory of this house that when the Dominion of Canada agreed to a treaty which was made between Great Britain and Japan, it was held that it had thereby divested the province of British Columbia of legislative power to restrict the character and the type of persons who might be employed upon government lands or mines. To that extent the legislature of the province of British Columbia was deprived of its legislative power because of the provisions of a treaty to which this country had given its approval. In my own mind I have never been satisfied as to how far the parliament of the Dominion of Canada had jurisdiction to deal with these problems, in view of the fact that we became a party to the treaty of Versailles and thereby, to that extent at least, interfered with the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces to whatever extent might be necessary to give effect to the provisions of the treaty. Whether or not the decision in the British Columbia case is of such far-reaching significance I am not at the moment prepared to say. In this regard I cannot but think what governments do just before an election and the alacrity with which their supporters will stand in their places and confer benedictions for their action is amazing when, as a matter of fact, as in this case this country was committed in the most solemn manner known to the law-by treaty-to do so many, many years ago what, we are now doing.
It was not the present government which made this treaty or which committed itself to these obligations; it was a government that was not led by a Liberal prime minister which made these commitments. At the international conference to which I have referred, employers and employees were represented,

Fair Wages and Hours
and I took the trouble the other day to search in the library, and I found there the record of the meeting of the first League of Nations international labour conference. I have in my hand the minutes of the first annual meeting held from October 29 to November 29, 1919. Looking at the record which indicates those who were present, I find that Canada was represented by the Hon. Gideon D. Robertson, Senator and Minister of Labour of Canada, the Hon. Newton W. Rowell, K.C., M.P., President of the Privy Council of Canada and Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. In the list of advisers I find the names of the following:
Mr. F. A. Acland, Deputy Minister of Labour of Canada.
Mr. Loring C. Christie, legal adviser to the Department of External Affairs of Canada.
Mr. Daniel A. Cameron, member of the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia.
The Hon. C. W. Robinson, minister without portfolio of the government of the province of New Brunswick,-
who is now a senator,
The Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, C.M.G., M.P., former Minister of Labour of Canada.
Mr. Louis Guyon, Deputy Minister of Labour for the province of Quebec.
Dr. Walter A. Riddell, Deputy Minister of Labour for the province of Ontario.
The Hon. Thomas H. Johnson. Attorney General for the province of Manitoba.
Sir. T. M. Molloy, secretary of the Bureau of Labour for the province of Saskatchewan.
The Hon. C. R. Mitchell, provincial treasurer of the province of Alberta.
Mr. J. D. McNiven, Deputy Minister of Labour for the province of British Columbia.
Mr. Gerald H. Brown, secretary of the Reconstruction Committee of the government of Canada.
The employers' delegate was Mr. S. R. Parsons, president of the British American Oil Company, Limited. The advisers are given as follows:
Mr. .T. E. Walsh, general manager, Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
Mr. J. T. Stirrett, general secretary, Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
Mr. E. Blake Robertson, Ottawa representative, Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
Mr. J. B. Hugg, Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
Mr. J. G. Merrick, secretary, Canadian Employers' Association.
The workers' delegate was Mr. P. M. Draper, secretary-treasurer, Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, and president of the Ottawa Typographical Union. The advisers are given as follows:
Mr. Tom Moore, president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
Mr. Arthur Martel, vice-president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
Mr. Robert Baxter, vice-president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
Mr. David Rees, vice-president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada.
Mrs. Kathleen Derry, member of the Boot and Shoe Workers' Union.
About fifty nations of the world were represented at that conference, and by looking at the index one may observe the long discussion which took place in connection with the eight hour day. I think it is only fair to say that at that conference which took place ten years ago last fall the universal opinion was expressed-probably I should not put it so strongly-the general opinion was expressed by resolution that the forty-eight hour week should be the prevailing period of work for those who toil. The question of terms of contract partly dealt with in the legislation now before the house is something which has been dealt with by order in council since and to some extent before that time.
There are two or three matters with which this bill does not in my opinion sufficiently deal. It is idle to say that you do not desire to be unfair to those who make contracts with the state; no nation desires to be unfair with those who undertake to work for it. There used to be an old saying with which those of you who have read law and those who have read a great deal of general literature will be familiar: " the infallible justice of the crown"-that the crown will never do an unjust act. I referred to such an incident the other day, where a well known firm of contractors alleged that they had suffered almost bankruptcy because of changes imposed by the Minister of Labour in the compensation paid to their workmen, and that indicates the possibilities of injustice being done. I express no opinion as to the correctness of their claim; I merely mention it. This bill as it now stands makes it possible for an injustice to be done, and I trust that before the minister finally settles his bill he will afford an opportunity to those who are greatly interested in matters of this kind to present their point of view to this house. I have had a large number of telegrams from employers and employees; from workmen and from the employers of workmen. Some of them, not understanding the terms of the bill, thought it was going to work a very great hardship at a point where clearly none was possible; others were very anxious that the bill should be enacted because they felt that it would afford them a measure of relief which clearly, under its terms, it does not afford.
As I i^ad the bill, it does not attempt to deal with the conflict in legislative power between the legislatures of the provinces on the one hand and the parliament of Canada on the other. Admitting that the principle

Fair Wages and Hours

of the bill is agreed to-and for my part I find it difficult to think that in this year 1930 any member of parliament should quarrel with the principle when repeatedly since 1920 this parliament has approved, in the most formal way at times and in informal ways at other times, of the principle of the measure-it becomes important to endeavour to work out the details in order to do no injustice either to the employer or to the employee. The first ipriniciple is the eight-hour day, and the second principle is a fair day's pay for a fair day's work. The one involves merely the measurement of time, which is not difficult; it is done with a clock or a watch. The other, the determination of the measure or the quantum of wages that shall be paid at given points is, of course, very difficult, and the minister has been very frank about that. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stated, he uses the word "current", which is a word susceptible to almost any meaning it may 'be desired to give to it.
In my judgment there should be something more specific than that when you come to deal with the question of tenders and contracts. For instance, if a tender is called for the construction of a post office in Nova Scotia and on the same day a tender is called for the construction of a post office in British Columbia and there is in each tender a provision stating that the contractor will be expected to comply with the provisions of the Fair Wage Act, he could not employ his workmen for more than eight hours per day. However, it might well be that the wages paid in Nova Scotia would not be at all the same as those paid in British Columbia. I think the minister has made that abundantly clear. I am not asserting for a single moment that you can have a uniform standard of wages throughout Canada, without taking notice of local conditions and the circumstances under which the work is performed. I do suggest, however, that in all such matters as these1, where tenders are called for public works, there should be at least some exactitude, for as I gathered from what the minister said this afternoon, if a change were to take place in current wages at a given point, then the contractor probably would have a good claim for extras by reason of the minister having exercised the powers mentioned.
I submit that should not be so, having regard to the maxim to which I referred, "the infallible justice of the crown", f^pd having regard to what was said by the privy council in the very early days of this confederation in a case which came from this Dominion. There the question was whether or not prop-

erty that had been taken should be compensated for, and the law lords pointed out that it must be presumed at all times that where benefits accrue to the crown, the crown is to pay for them. If a contractor, having in mind the terms of such a contract as I have mentioned, tenders and is successful; if the contract is signed containing the terms I have indicated, the minister, in the exercise of the powers now contemplated by this measure, may impose upon that contractor a burden which might amount to thousands of dollars more than he contemplated when he made his tender. Surely then he would be entitled to a claim for extras. I would say that would be reasonably clear at any rate, and certainly in my younger days, when I was engaged with corporations which had to deal with conditions of this kind, under similar circumstances they regarded the claim for extras as being well founded. I remember one case in particular in connection with the digging of the irrigation ditch near Calgary, in which such a claim was accepted at once by the railway company because it was felt that conditions had changed, through no fault of the contractor, and had imposed upon him an added burden. The benefit of the extra work having accrued to the railway company they were willing to pay, and in fact did pay.
The next principle in this measure is one which I suggest should be carefully considered by this house. If hon. gentlemen present will take the trouble to look at the last section of the measure, which is section 5, they will observe that very great powers are conferred upon the minister, to the exercise of which there is no limit. When I say "limit" I mean there is no reasonable limit as to the extent to which they may be exercised. Now, whatever may be said of human progress, I think at least it can be truthfully observed that today there is a tendency to limit the exercise of power by the executive and to rely more and more upon the exercise of power by the legislation branch of government. When one observes the provisions of section 5 it is seen that upon the representation and recommendation of the minister, resulting in an order in council, there is conferred upon the government of this country a power which might be tyrannical and which certainly would be autocratic. It is a power to make regulations dealing with almost every factor that might arise in the enforcement of the provisions of the statute itself, and if my hon. friend the Minister of Labour will be good enough to look at the last subsection, namely subsection (j), he will observe these words:
generally for the due enforcement of the provisions of the act and the regulations.

Fair Waj/es and Hours
In other words, this parliament is being asked to give to the minister a letter of credit which will enable him not only to pass regulations dealing with the various defined subjects in the statute but also to enforce the provisions of the statute itself as well as those of the regulations. Not only is he given the power to enforce, but he is given power to make regulations beyond enforcement.

And penalties
also.

And that involves, my
hon. friend has said, the question of penalties as well. Now, I ask my hon. friend the Prime Minister if it is sound legislation to ask parliament to confer these powers upon any minister, regardless of his politics. I leave out that question for the moment, because I am treating the Minister of Labour as an office and not as an individual at all. In this day is it sound legislation to confer powers upon one man, with the aid of a government passing an order in council, such as this section contemplates?
That is the third principle in this legislation. I am powerless, of course, to prevent such a section being enacted; I am entirely powerless to prevent it from becoming the law of Canada, but I am not powerless to present my protest against such arbitrary powers being conferred upon the holder of any office. Twice during this session of parliament I have had occasion to refer to what Lord Chief Justice Hewart terms his essay, but which in fact is a volume of considerable size. I refer again to The New Despotism, and in discussing the matter Lord Hewart refers to a number of cases decided by the courts in England in which they strongly criticize the exercise of this power by the executive branch of government. It is fatal to the development of our institutions; certainly it is fatal to democracy that any parliament should confer upon any office-and I am not now dealing with the hon. gentleman who holds the office-such an arbitrary power clothed with the possibilities of the tyrannical exercise of that power. I do not contemplate that that will be the case, but he is clothed with the possibility of exercising such tyrannical power, and I say it is subversive of the very freedom and liberty this parliament should possess, and is inimical to the interests of the people themselves.
The work of Lord Hewart deals with this matter in detail. By an odd circumstance, before the book had actually left the hands of the printers, although advance copies had been circulated, when a review had appeared, 2419-91J
the Lord Chancellor was so impressed that he appointed a committee to investigate all the recent statutes passed in England, for the purpose of ascertaining the extent to which parliament had divested itself of authority and conferred upon officials such enormous powers as the powers indicated by section 5 of this bill. I trust the minister will pause before he asks this parliament to give him powers so great. I am not for one moment objecting to those powers being exercised by this minister, but I have objected consistently to such powers being exercised by any minister. I consider the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) a fair minded minister, but I do not .think that it is in the interests of Canada that powers so great should be conferred upon any one individual under the modem democratic form of government where the temptations for abuse are as great as the powers here conferred.
The introduction of this bill at this time indicates what pressure will do in a democracy. Ten years had passed and this bill had not been introduced; it was not introduced by the predecessors of the hon. minister. It is perfectly true that the session after August, 1919, was more of a tentative nature than other sessions; it is perfectly true that the government of that day was defeated; the government of Sir Robert Borden disappeared and Mr. Meighen assumed office, and in 1921 he was defeated. There has been no opportunity since 1922 for any government other than a Liberal government to enact legislation of this nature, and the very fact that it has not been enacted up to this date indicates two things. The first is the confusion-using that word in no offensive sense-as between the relative legislative powers of the legislatures of the provinces and the parliament of the Dominion, and the other is the hesitancy to approach the solution of a problem under the terms and regulations of a treaty and of subsequent international conferences, because there are varying conditions in this country from east to west and there are varying ideas as to whether or not the terms of the treaty correctly interpret the opinion of the people of Canada.
I have said before, and I say it here again, that criticisms may be urged in some localities against this measure, and criticisms may be urged by some occupations. The farmer very probably may say that he has no eight hour day; the right hon. the Prime Minister very probably may say that he has no eight hour day, and the professional men may say the same thing. We have various classes which will contend that a statutory enact-
Fair Wages and Hours

msnt which imposes an eight hour day as the period during which labour shall be carried on by men engaged in certain activities, does violence to the known conditions under which men of other classes have to toil for hours varying from eight to eighteen.
There are many matters in connection with the passing of this legislation which in themselves are good reasons why the principle enunciated in section 5 should not be adopted, such as, pressure of circumstances, pressure of political friends, the pressure which arises from the contemplation of an early election and the desirability of securing the support of known classes in communities-all these things are known to us. Why endeavour to deceive ourselves? We kaow perfectly well that in many instances the government is influenced by circumstances, and human nature being as it is, that always will be so. The government must consider the necessity of securing support at the polls for their candidates at the approaching elections.
I would venture to suggest again to the hon. gentleman the desirability, nay the necessity, of this parliament considering carefully before it forces upon any officer, however eminent he may be or however fair-minded he may be, powers so great, so fraught with opportunities for tyranny, the exercise of which is repugnant to the very idea of our institutions, of the conventions and of the treaty itself which brought about the possibility of an international declaration for a forty-eight-hour week and an eight-hour day at fair wages.

In connection with the extras allowed to contractors, is it not a fact that the rates of wages are made known to the contractor before he signs the contract? I simply mention that because in the case of the Calgary post office the rates of wages were set and were known to the contractor before he signed the contract so that he would have no claim for extras in that regard.

I am certainly very grateful to my hon. friend for bringing that to my attention, because it was in view of the terms of this statute which we are now considering that I was directing attention to the danger. Subsection (a) of section 3 reads:
All persv ntt in the employ of the contractor, subcontractor, or of any other person doing or contracting to do the whole or any part of the work contemplated by the contract shall be paid such wages as are generally accepted as current from time to time for competent workmen in the district in which the work is being performed for the character or class of work in which they are respectively engaged; provided that wages shall in all cases be such as are fair and reasonable.
[Mr. Dennett.)
On reference to the section conferring upon the minister the powers to which I have referred, it will be observed that the minister has power to regulate the method of determining what are current or fair and reasonable wages and the preparation and use of schedules of rates relating thereto; rates of wages for overtime; classifications of employment or work; the publication and posting of wage schedules. It will be observed that the power conferred upon the minister by the bill and the regulations authorize him to make a variation from time to time in the rate of wages, and it is because of that difficulty-it is a real one and not an imaginary one-that I point out the desirability of having something in the form of a schedule, either definite as the hon. gentleman has suggested, or at least providing in definite terms for the rates of wages, so that a claim for extras would not be a matter of grace or favour, but a matter of right to the contractor who has imposed upon him a higher wage rate than that which he had in mind and which appeared in the schedule upon which he prepared his tender and upon which the contract was awarded. The contractor would have a just claim for extras which the government should pay for the services rendered.
I am quite sure that when the right hon. the Prime Minister considers this section and recalls the observations he made as to the desirability of restricting rather than extending the powers of the executive branch of government-even in times of war complaint was made that those powers were too extensive -he will find that in times of peace the exercise of this power is fraught with the gravest danger.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on the second reading of this bill, but I think it is perhaps only fair to the minister himself, in view of what the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has just said as to arbitrary powers being given by this legislation to the minister, to point out that the purpose of the section to which my hon. friend has referred is diametrically the opposite to that of conferring any arbitrary power. The section might have been worded:
That the Minister of Labour may make regulations with regard to wages and hours herein provided for and without limiting the generality of the foregoing may provide by regulation for,-
If that had been the wording of the section the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition would have been most apposite,

Fair Wages and Hours
but it does not say anything of the kind; it specifically restricts the power for the making of these regulations to the governor in council.
Upon the recommendation of the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly, upon the recommendation of the minister; every order in council is made upon the recommendation of some minister. The appropriate minister to make a recommendation with respect to any act is the minister by whose department the act is being administered. But my hon. friend will, I am sure, agree that because a minister brings in a recommendation to council, it does not necessarily follow that council automatically accepts and passes the recommendation. If that is the method in which orders in council have been passed in any government with which my hon. friend has been associated, I can assure him that it is not the method followed by the present administration. Ministers frequently have the greatest difficulty in getting their recommendations adopted by their colleagues and not infrequently fail entirely so to do. That is the distinct merit of our system of government in which the cabinet plays the important part it does. It prevents the will or wish of any individual who may happen to have a special interest which he desires to have promoted, prevailing at the expense of those who entertain opposite points of view or who are trying to protect other interests unless the object is obviously one wholly in the public interest.	,
What happens when a minister brings his recommendation to council is that the recommendation is very carefully scrutinized by all his colleagues. The Minister of Finance looks at the recommendation from the point of view of what it involves in the way of expenditure. The Minister of Railways looks at it from the point of view of how it is going to affect employees on government railroads or those which may be in competition with government roads. The Minister of Agriculture has his thought immediately directed to the conditions in the agricultural industry and he compares the effect of any suggested regulation with what is likely as a consequence to arise in that particular industry. So one might continue to mention all of the various points of view that are represented around a council table. The fact that authority is given to the governor in council and not to the minister is for the very purpose of avoiding the thing to which
my hon. friend is taking exception, namely, giving to any single minister arbitrary power.
May I point out that with respect to any legislation there are usually all-important details with regard to which parliament is not as well qualified to deal as a department of the government or the governor in council. Take, for example, the various matters mentioned in this bill as matters which must be considered by the governor in council:
The method of determining what are current or fair and reasonable wages and the preparation and use of schedules of rates relating thereto.
Parliament might spend weeks in discussing what it is best to do in that regard and yet not find a solution that would really suit the circumstances of each case, for the simple reason that the law will apply to all parts of the Dominion, at all seasons of the year, under all circumstances and it would be almost impossible for parliament to anticipate some of the situations which will arise, but which, nevertheless, will have to be regulated in accordance with some general principle or rule. Take another item:
The publication and posting of wage schedules.
This is a question with which parliament surely would not wish to concern itself, for example, as to whether wage schedules were to be published in the Labour Gazette or the Canada Gazette, whether they were to be published in the form of bulletins to be posted on the works themselves or exhibited in some other way. Those are details with which the department itself can deal satisfactorily, but as regards which parliament would be only wasting its time if it sought to express any opinion beyond that of indicating in the legislation itself its desire to see that that particular feature is given attention.
The keeping of proper books and records and the examination of the same by government officers.
The fact that parliament mentions that the keeping of proper records is a subject with which the governor in council deals means, not that parliament is parting with any legislative power or control, but rather that parliament wishes to indicate that this particular feature (should receive attention and the working out of it be left to a proper government department. It would be only occupying the time of the house unnecessarily to run through the other regulations as they are all much of the same nature.
To return to what I said at the outset: far from giving the minister autocratic powers, the purpose of the section in giving authority to the governor in council is so to circum-
143S
Fair Wages and Hours

scribe the minister that no single individual in the government, however worthy he may be or however worthy may be the cause that he represents, will have the opportunity of arbitrarily fixing rules and regulations, but will have to submit whatever he suggests to a jury, if I may term it as such, representative of all bodies of opinion in the country.
It is the executive branch and not the legislative branch of government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; but when a minister is submitting his regulations to his colleagues in council, to all intents and purposes he is appearing before his peers and making out a case if he is able so to do.
My hon. friend speaks about government by order in council. I am entirely of his point of view that government by order in council should be restricted; that the supremacy of parliament is all-important. But there is a great difference between having general legislative power given in a statute to deal with any and all subjects by order in council and having power given under a particular statute to pass orders in council for the purpose of carrying out the objects of a particular statute. When I was seated in opposition where my hon. friend is at the present time and took such strong exception to government by order in council, it was because the government of that day had, because of war conditions, received from parliament under a War Measures Act power to deal by order in council with almost any subject; and were continuing in peace time to proceed under that measure: they had not repealed the statute which gave them power to legislate generally by order in council as I think it should have been repealed immediately the war was over, if indeed, it should ever have been introduced or applied as extensively as it was. That was the reason exception was taken, but that is a very different matter from taking exception to parliament enacting a measure for any specific purpose and in the measure itself giving to a minister of the crown or to the governor in council power to pass the necessary orders to see that the specific piece of legislation itself is carried out. So far as this act is concerned, parliament is doing something that is very clear and direct, something which it would appear is generally approved, namely, establishing an eight hour day so far as most of the construction under government contracts and the government's own employees are concerned, and directing that the wages paid to the government's own employees on works of construction and the

like connected with our public works, shall be wages that are fair and reasonable. That is the principle and purpose of the measure. In passing the second reading, in adopting that principle, parliament has gone about as far as it is possible to go by way of necessary legislation, beyond giving to some authority what may be necessary by way of making the essential proper regulations to achieve these ends. I submit, so far as the regulations are concerned, that the clauses drafted circumscribe pretty effectively the action of any minister who may seek to be autocratic.

Mr. Speaker, while I can agree in general with the principle of the bill, there are one or two points in connection therewith which I desire to discuss. No hon. member will contend for a moment that the time is not long past due for the introduction of a measure of this character. I think the first time that labour representations to this effect were made to this government was as far back as 1925. There had been representations even before that time, but for considerably more than ten years, as the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said, this government or the preceding one has had before it proposals of this character. The eight hour day is on the one hand, just a small attempt to meet the increasing problem of the displacement of men by machinery, and on the other it is an effort on the part of those who advocate it to lessen the innumerable accidents which are becoming so great a burden on industry and the state. According to both medical authorities and other scientific investigators, long hours of labour have not only the effect of lessening the vigour and vitality of those so engaged, but towards the closing hour the percentage of accidents among men working long hours so strikingly increases that one can no longer doubt that the excessively long working day has been and is a major factor in industrial accidents. It has also been responsible for the high cost of accident insurance. The state as a whole, in my opinion, will gain by the introduction of this measure. Every industry in Canada would be well advised to follow the example set by this legislation by introducing at least the eight hour work day.
We have had in recent years the illustration of the burnt-out soldier, but few of us have discussed the existence of the bumt-out industrial worker. Yet as the result of high pressure work and long hours of labour men become so mentally and physically devitalized that after the age of forty many of them are no longer desired by industrial employers.

There is no doubt whatever that that has been one of the principal factors in our present unemployment problem. A study of the ages of those employed in industry in the province of Ontario will indicate that the average ranges from twenty-eight to thirty-five years of age. It is a fact that industry is increasingly requiring the services of young men who are capable of making quick adjustments of machinery rather than those who through long study have become experts in some branch of technical work. The long working day has also unquestionably been a factor in increasing the percentage' of men who drink after they leave work exhausted and devitalized. No condition of the human body has so great a tendency to cause a man to thirst for an artificial stimulant of some kind as the exhaustion experienced after a long day's work, and on that ground the government is well advised in introducing this legislation. I notice that the Prime Minister smiles; I am quite certain he is not smiling at the underlying fact.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was smiling at my hon. friend's thought of the need for stimulants after a long day.

Industrial scientists in Great Britain, after making an exhaustive inquiry into and prolonged experimentation bearing upon the question of the maximum physical efficiency of the worker in relation to hours of work came to the conclusion that efficiency can best be reached by working a week of forty hours or less, and that once the forty hour week is exceeded, efficiency begins to decrease with every additional hour. Statistics in other countries show, as I have already mentioned, that the number of industrial accidents tends to increase after a certain number of hours of labour and that by far the highest percentage of accidents occurs in what is called the penultimate hour of the day's work. This, of course, is undoubtedly due to the lack of muscular control of the individual exhausted by excessive hours of labour.
One other reason in my opinion why this bill should pass the house unanimously is that it is but a long-deferred redeeming of our definite pledges in this matter. The national honour is at stake. That may seem almost a theatrical statement, but I feel sincerely, Mr. Speaker, that the national honour has been questioned for some time because of our apparent indifference to the promises we made over our signature in connection with these labour conventions.
Fair Wages and Hours
I now come specifically to the bill itself, and I refer the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour to section 3, which reads:
Every contract with the government of Canada for construction, remodelling, repair or demolition of any work shall be subject to the following conditions respecting wages and hours:
That is all that is provided in the bill with regard to hours of labour. It is narrowed down to contracts. What about the penitentiary employees, men who to-day are working a shift of nine hours? Are they not to be included in this measure? What about the hospital orderlies in our own institutions who now work an eleven-hour day and a thirteen-hour night in alternate shifts? What about mechanics, machinists, electricians and many others? What about the employees of the Canadian National railway system, some of whom are working over eight hours a day? Frankly, Mr. Speaker, if I have any criticism of the measure it is that it does not go nearly far enough. I at hand have other illustrations with respect to employees of the government on the St. Lawrence waterway development, I find that many are working twelve hours a day. I grant you that there may be extenuating circumstances in the case of lockmasters. There are some lockmasters, however, whose hours of work should not be more than eight per day because of the character of the work which they have to do in that eight hours Of course, there are others who one day will have nothing to do and the next day may have to lock only a few boats through, but these are not the usual run of cases.
I say therefore, Mr. Speaker, in the first place, that because health is one of the foundations of the state, and because health is in a measure affected by excessive hours of work, this bill will tend to improve conditions and will therefore receive my support. Further, I am in favour of it because the loss of human life increases with longer hours of labour; because long hours of labour have a tendency to degrade by devitalizing human beings; because the state should be the first to recognize the value of the health and happiness of the worker, and because the mechanization of industry has created a real additional reason why the hours of labour should be reduced. But I would ask the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister to take into consideration the point that I have raised with regard to the appearance of limitation in section 3 of the bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That has already been done by order in council. I think it covers the other classes.
Fair Wages and Hours

It covers
all classes on federal work?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
I am delighted to know it. I remember now that the minister did bring in some measure purporting to have that effect, but I had overlooked it.

Am I to conclude from
the remarks of the hon. member that he would like the eight hour day applied to railway employees?
I know it is applied to the greater part of the railway employees' work. What particular point does my hon. friend desire to make?
They are paid overtime after eight hours.

My hon.
friend apparently was tiying to trip me up. I wish to direct the attention of the Minister of Labour to a particular type of employment to which consideration should be given. I will take a point like Drumheller in Alberta. The postmaster is engaged and paid by the Post Office Department. I take it that the postmaster engages his own help, at least if not in every case in most cases. I find that the workers employed by the postmaster are frequently compelled to work long hours and under most unfair conditions. I made some inquiries recently into the situation at Drumheller, which is in my constituency, and I find that work in the post office commences between 7.00 and 7.80 a.m. and concludes with the finish of the working day at 7.00 p.m.; that is a period of approximately twelve hours. One hour is permitted for lunch and an average of twenty-five minutes only for the evening meal.
That is not under regulations of the department.

I realize
that. That is why I am raising the question.
I think some provision should be made to take care of cases of this kind. Not only are the people working in an exceedingly ill-fitted, badly ventilated and wholly unsuitable building-may I now congratulate the government on having recognized that and decided to remedy the condition-but the sanitary arrangements are utterly insufficient, and the result has been that some of the female helpers have had to undergo medical treatment. Here is a statement in regard to that: Due to the latter hazard, periodical lay-offs by the employees are frequent, and medical 
advice is to the effect that the conditions of employment are responsible for these lay-offs. One girl tells me that the doctor advised more fresh air and shorter hours of labour, and this appears to be the usual prescription.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of that, may I ask the Minister of Labour to take into consideration some measure which would look after the indirect employees of departments like the Post Office Department of whom advantage is taken by the direct employees of the government? I may say that the principle of the bill is satisfactory to me, and I only wish it went further.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

I have, I suppose in common with many other members of the house, received telegrams suggesting that an opportunity should be afforded to those who are vitally affected to present their views. As the bill proceeds in committee, before it finally is disposed of it did occur to me that possibly the minister might allow the bill to go to one of the standing committees to have representations made by those who feel an injustice is being done to them with respect to some of the sections dealing with contracts and the right of the minister to increase wages from time to time-the very point mentioned by my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) In view of those representations it strikes me it might be desirable to afford that opportunity to those who are under this misapprehension.

Yesterday'' at noon there
assembled in this city a large delegation representing the manufacturers' association and contractors. It appeared to me they had a wrong conception of the purpose of the bill, and after we had discussed the bill for an hour and a half it was made quite clear to them that the bill was not intended to apply to factories. When I assured them that if there was any doubt about this a subsection would be introduced to make it perfectly clear, they went away fairly satisfied-of course, I would not say one hundred per cent satisfied, because my hon. friend will realize that the average employer of labour does not care for legislation such as this. As for the changing of the rate of wages after the contract has been signed, it has been the policy of the government of Canada for the past thirty years.

To change wages from
time to time?

Fair Wages and Hours

Yes. Except in probably
a couple of cases, one of which my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, mentioned this afternoon, it does not appear that this has resulted in any great hardship or injustice being done to employers. I am satisfied, as my hon. friend well said, that the government of Canada, no matter what party might be in power, would deal justly with both employers and employees. As I said, there have been two instances where the rate of wages has been changed after the contract had been signed. I recall that in 1913 or 1914 circumstances arose in connection with a contract which required the contractor to pay higher wages than were provided for, and my hon. friends themselves before going out of office in 1921 compensated the contractor for the extra cost, although they need not necessarily have done so under the terms of the contract, but I presume they felt it was fair and right that compensation should be granted. At the present time, as my hon. friend has stated, there is a claim against the government under a contract because of the rate of wages having been increased, notwithstanding the fact that the present fair wage regulations make the minister's decision final in the matter. I am satisfied that the minister of labour in any government would be perfectly within his rights in recommending to his colleagues whatever might seem to him just in relation to either contractor or employees. With respect to the Welland canal contract which I believe the hon. member had in mind, the decision of the Minister of Labour has been submitted to a commission for consideration. The present minister has no hesitation in taking such a course.
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition seems to think that clause 5 gives too much arbitrary power to the minister. As the Prime Minister pointed out, it extends only so far as the cabinet by order in council may specify what powers the Minister of Labour may have in the matter; and inasmuch as this practice has prevailed for almost thirty years, and very little injustice has been done to any contractors, I think my hon. friend will agree that no injustice will be done while the present Minister of Labour is in office-which will be so long as he or I remain in public life during the next forty years.
My hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) admitted, I think, that he had forgotten that this bill was only a part of the program of the government as to the eight hour principle, because he spoke with respect to employees directly engaged by the government and not working for contractors. I want to draw my hon. friend's attention to the order in council that was passed on March 27, 1930.
What day was it tabled in the house?
I am not so sure about that; it was a couple of days after.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think it was the same or next day.

It was within a couple of days anyway. I wish to put on Hansard a certified copy of a minute of the meeting of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on March 27, 1930.
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 19th March, 1930, from the Minister of Labour, submitting as follows:-
1.	That it was recognized in the labour part of the treaty of Versailles and the corresponding provisions of the other treaties of peace, that the well-being-physical, moral and intellectual-of industrial wage earners is of supreme international importance, and that although differences of climate, habits and customs, economic principles and industrial traditions, make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of immediate attainment, there are methods and principles for regulating labour conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
2.	That approval was expressed in the peace treaties of the principle of the eight hour working day.
3.	That a draft convention was adopted at the first session of the conference of the international labour organization (League of Nations) in 1919 to limit hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight hours per day.
4.	That the draft convention above mentioned was referred in 1924 to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons of Canada for examination and report.
5.	That on the recommendation of the committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons, approved by the House of Commons, the draft convention on hours of work in industrial undertakings was referred by order in council to the Supreme Court of Canada with a view to determining the jurisdiction of the federal and provincial authorities, respectively, on this subject.
6.	That the judgment of the Supreme Court, of Canada contained the following declaration. "The subject matter is generally within^ the competence of the legislatures of the provinces but the authority vested in these legislatures does not enable them to give the force of law to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention in relation to servants of the Dominion government, or to legislate for those parts of Canada which are not within the boundaries of a province."

The conclusions of the investigation may be briefly summarized as follows:

manufactured, for the most part, on premises other than those of the government contractors, and according to one of the three modes of subcontracting already described. As a result of this the government contractors have had no immediate supervision of the contract work, and have, in fact, only assumed a partial responsibility for the methods and conditions under which it was performed. In other words, the contractors, while reaping the benefits of the contract in question, have failed to discharge adequately the duties and responsibilities which may not unfairly be regarded as appertaining to the proper carrying out of their obligations.
2.	Most of the work on government clothing has really been executed by women and girls. Where these have been employed in shops their wages have been, on the whole, exceedingly low; and where the work was performed in homes the prices paid were often such as to necessitate long hours of labour for a very meagre return. In the case of those employed by subcontractors the general rule has been to require a maximum amount of work for a minimum amount of pav. Exceptionally long hours and other objectionable features have marked the course of the employment of the workers in the homes and of not a few in the shops.

The introduction of a subcontractor, who lesorts to hired help, has involved the necessity of realizing a double profit out of the work of the hands and, as a consequence of this and the competition of subcontractors, the wages of the large majority of those engaged in government work have suffered a considerable depression. We pledged our solemn word in the Versailles treaty that we would stand by the principle of the eight hour day. We are expecting the other nations to stand by their obligations, and yet we have not been able to carry out our own solemn obligation. If we are given the authority to make a treaty I should say, although I do not happen to be an international lawyer, that we have a certain responsibility for carrying out the terms of that treaty.
