But, as I suggested to him this afternoon, when the bill first went into committee, an opportunity should be afforded to those interested to satisfy themselves with regard to this measure. I am unable to determine the effect of the amendments without seeing them in the bill, and I am unable to realize their relation to the other clauses of the bill. I would suggest to the minister that if the bill is now reported it should be reprinted with the two amendments before it is given the third reading, so that we may be able to understand fully the operation of the proposed legislation. Then it could not be said, because of difficulties which might arise in the future, that we had neglected the duty devolving upon us with respect to legislation giving effect to an international treaty, the greatest the world has ever known.
I was unable to understand what the hon. minister had in mind when he went to such great lengths to show what somebody else had done some twenty years ago. The basis of this legislation is a treaty of peace between warring nations of the world, and when it was said the other day that the then prime minister, Sir Robert Borden, had taken an active interest in connection with the labour clauses of that treaty, the Prime Minister interjected some doubt as to whether or not he had ever seen those clauses. As a matter of fact that is not the record, and if he will take the trouble to inquire he will find that certain clauses in their present form were attributable to the work of revision by Sir Robert Borden. That is not secondhand evidence, and the right hon. gentleman can satisfy himself upon that point. Why go back to show what somebody else had in

Excise Act Amendment

his mind years ago, unless the purpose was as I indicated this afternoon? The minister's purpose was so apparent that I think it my duty to expose it.
The only other matter which remains for consideration is whether or not the legislation itself gives effect to the provisions of the treaty, and of the international conferences which were held under the treaty, in such a way as to protect alike the interests of employers and employees. As I said this afternoon, employers were represented as well as employees at the first international labour conference held by the League of Nations, and since the minister does not seem disposed to send this bill to a committee for consideration, I suggest that before the third reading it be reprinted in order that some of us who are interested may be able clearly to understand whether or not under the decision of the supreme court parliament is overstepping the powers which the provinces enjoy. As I said to the minister this afternoon, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was not present, I have always had grave doubts of the effect of section 92 of the British North America Act conferring exclusive legislative jurisdiction upon the provinces with respect to international treaties, having regard to the decision of the privy council in the British Columbia case. That point does not seem to have been considered by the supreme court in connection with the reference made to it regarding the relative jurisdiction of the provinces and the Dominion to enact an eight hour day law or provide for a forty-eight hour week.
Bill reported.

Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill
No. 48, to amend the Excise Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-Power to examine on oath.

As the minister proceeds may I ask him whether he does not think there is a possibility of substituting as judges officers of the department who necessarily are charged with a sense of their own responsibility? That is the only observation I had in mind in connection with this proposed legislation when I read the bill. Does the minister follow me?
I do.

Power is given to summon witnesses, to pay the expenses of such witnesses, and to arrive at conclusions mostly judicial in character. That power is given to officers of the department who cannot be said to be other than charged with the responsibility of securing convictions for breaches of the law.

Even under the amendment
as it stands in the bill, this power would not be given to inferior officers of the department, if I may so term them. It confines the power pretty well to what are known as superior officers. My deputy informs me that in the interpretation of the act this means inspectors, and of course the commissioner or the assistant commissioner. The amendment is designed more particularly for use in instances in which an investigation is desired at remote places throughout the Dominion where a commissioner is not readily obtainable. I think I may assure the committee there will be no disposition to abuse this power and if the investigation were of major importance probably we would proceed in the usual way and appoint a commissioner.
An opportunity will undoubtedly be afforded to the persons affected to appear, if they so desire, and present their side of any inquiry that may be made?
Quite so. I might add further for the information of the committee this is based on a provision in the Post Office Act and I do not think it is abused there.

I once assisted in an
inquiry under it and the question of an opportunity to be heard is very important.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Neglecting to keep books, making false returns, etc.

I notice that under this
clause there are certain statements with regards to fines for infringements of the law. There is no provision for imprisonment if people offend more than once.

The matter will be one for
the courts.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Removing bonded goods without entry.

This is a departure from
the existing law. Will the minister make a statement about it?

Excise Act Amendment

It is really similar to the
amendment proposed in clause 3. We are proposing to make the removal of goods from bonded warehouses without authorization an indicatable offence in order to regularize what we have had just a bit of doubt about. We want to be able under the law to seize the goods. In the past we have done so, basing our right upon the provision respecting "fraud upon the revenue." We are not quite satisfied that this offence constitutes a fraud upon the revenue within the meaning of the act, and we simply want to regularize a practice which we have been following in the past.

Section agreed to.
Section 5 agreed to.
On section 6-Proceedings against party.
This provision is exactly the same as the one in the Customs Act. It is merely to harmonize the two.
This is not a provision which I like. What has been the experience of the department in the working out of the similar section of the Customs Act?

The experience of the department with regard to the Excise Act has been that where we thought it was perfectly plain that the onus of proving certain things lay upon the person in possession of the goods, magistrates in their wisdom, rightly or wrongly, insisted that we must prove illegal manufacture or illegal importation. This is an effort on the part of the law officers of the crown to make certain what we thought already was certain. I may say our law officers only hope this will do what we already thought was in force.
It is pretty drastic.
We already have it in the Customs Act.
Was it taken from the Ontario Temperance Act?
It is exactly the same section the minister put into the Customs Act a couple of years ago to meet a difficulty which arose in the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia.
Yes.

Section agreed to.
Sections 7, 8 and 9 agreed to.
On section 10-Duties of excise on every pound of screened malt.

Will the minister explain the operation of this?
2419-92J
Mr. EULER. This is merely to institute a different practice in the collection of excise duty on malt. Where malt is imported from the United States it is already screened anc no difficulty arises with regard to it. But under our present practice the domestic product has excise charged upon it before the screening is done. We propose to impose the excise duty after the screening is done in order to relieve us of a good many orders in council making refunds or providing for the passage of a sufficient quantity of malt to compensate for what are called the coomings. It is merely a matter of adjustment in the department to make it a little easier for us, and I might add that it meets with the approval of the maltsters.

Section agreed to.
Sections 11 to 15 inclusive agreed to.
On section 16-Tobacco grown for private use.
What is that?

The grower of tobacco is now privileged without the payment of excise to make tobacco into the form of Canada twist. This will enable him to cut the tobacco for his own use without necessarily putting it in the form of Canada twist.

Section agreed to.
Section 17 agreed to.
On section 18-Alcohol made and treated in distilleries.
What is the effect of this section?
It merely provides that where the provincial government makes a seizure of liquor improperly produced, it must be surrendered to the Dominion authorities for destruction.

Is that sound? In view of the fact that alcohol for use in hospitals costs so much money, why should not there be some arrangement by which that alcohol could be given to the hospitals? I have had visits from those who have to provide the money for the purchase of alcohol for the hospitals for rubbing and medicinal purposes, and looking over the legislation casually, it occurred to me that condensed alcohol might well be given to the hospitals.
They now get a 99 per cent drawback.

I know; I am familiar with drawbacks. There are very few people
Excise Act Amendment

manufacturing in Canada who do not get drawbacks. But I am talking now about the consumer. It is one way of being free trade in practice and protectionist in theory, as the minister perhaps is well aware; at least, if he is not, he has forgotten more than I think he has. Another gentleman in the cabinet who is interested in drawbacks on coal used in salt works and dredging is not here to-night.
I think it desirable to consider whether that alcohol could not be given to hospitals and institutions of that kind. Here you have something that is worth money. It is seized because there has been a violation of the law, and it is to be destroyed. You compel the province to hand it over to the federal authorities for destruction. Now the province has property in it. I doubt very much whether we have the right to pass this section, because the province has the right to retain possession of that alcohol as part of the result of the operation of the law, it being something that the province has seized, and for which the offender has been convicted. The alcohol is legally in the possession of the province. Now you say that the province must hand it over to the federal authorities for destruction. I suggest that a very desirable way to deal with that difficulty is to give the alcohol to the hospitals for their use.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is it alcohol illegally manufactured that is under discussion?
This alcohol is well suited for the use of the hospitals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How do we know?
The authorities know because they seize it, and they seize it only because it has not been sufficiently adulterated as alcohol not to be called alcohol.
It is tested anyway.
Yes, and it is seized because it is alcohol.
When rubbing alcohol is purchased by the hospitals, they pay no excise at all.
I know, but-
So I do not see very much point in my hon. friend's suggestion.
But look at the price they have to pay for it.

We do not regulate the
price, and in every case they get 99 per cent drawback. A good deal of the liquors seized are not fit for hospital purposes. I should add .that I was in error when I said that the 
liquor must be handed over to the federal authorities in order to be destroyed. That is not exactly correct. It is denatured. In the province of Quebec when smuggled liquor is seized, we allow the commission to have it provided they pay the duty. In a case like this, where a province has seized the alcohol or whisky or liquor of some sort, the Dominion authorities certainly have a claim upon it because the excise should be satisfied. We want to make certain that alcohol of all sorts, no matter how produced or by whom seized, must pay its excise to the federal authorities. That is the point.

I still think that if the minister will have his legal officers advise him, they will tell him at once that the question I submit is not so easily disposed of as that. The crown in the right of the province has seized the alcohol, and of that property, by reason of legal condemnation, the crown in the right of the province has ownership. It therefore belongs to the province and not to the Dominion. You are now saying that the province must hand it over to the Dominion in order that the excise may be paid. You are either going to denature it or get your excise tax from it. To overcome that difficulty I suggest that you give it to the hospitals for their use. They will escape the excise tax and also escape buying something that is condemned. That property is vested in the crown in the right of the province. I doubt if this parliament has the right to take it away from the province. The minister has not quite appreciated the point.
Oh yes.

It is not so easily to be disposed of. The hon. minister's law is not always sound. This is property held by the crown in the right of the province by legal condemnation, which vests that property in the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the course of a commercial venture, and they are liable to pay tax.

The province get it by condemnation proceedings, and the property is the property of the crown in the right of the province by such condemnation proceedings-not for commercial purposes, but by reason of a seizure, a trial and a condemnation. One day a question may be raised in the courts as to the legality of the action, and I merely make my suggestion in order to get over the difficulty. This is a property which might be used for a useful purpose

Excise Act Amendment
without costing anything for the alcohol which is condemned or anything for excise which has never been paid. I suggest that it be given to the hospitals. If the minister knew just what it means to some of these hospitals to buy alcohol despite the rebate of the excise and other taxes, he would realize how important this becomes to them. I know what it means from the efforts I made years ago to have the present regulations enforced in connection with rebates of the duty paid upon such alcohol.

I do not want to prolong
the argument, Mr. Chairman, but I do not think the Department of Customs could yield this, that any alcohol produced in Canada or imported is not fairly subject to excise or customs duty. This particular clause arises from the fact that the government of one of the provinces had made a seizure of alcohol; we demanded possession, there was a lawsuit, and it was settled finally by our consenting to the province denaturing the alcohol.

How was the settlement
arrived at?
By agreement.
Exactly; and the agreement recognized the property rights of the province.

We consented to it rather
than have the lawsuit continued. I am not a constitutional lawyer, but this section has been introduced as an amendment on the advice of the deputy minister of Justice to make our rights perfectly clear to do what we say we intend to do. If we are wrong, and if the provinces choose to combat it and succeed before the courts, I shall have nothing to say.

Do you invite another
lawsuit?

Not at all; but I like to
maintain the rights of the department.

I can remember
when seized alcohol was given to charitable institutions. Six or seven years ago I was connected with a hospital and I was told that that was the practice.

My knowledge does not go
back as far as that, but I am assured by the Commisisoner of Excise, who has been in the department about forty odd years, that it never was done.

It is the custom in
Detroit, and I believe in the state of Michigan generally, when alcohol is seized to turn it over to the hospitals for hospital use. When they get hold of good whisky they turn that over also-for the use of the doctors.

I feel very strongly on
this matter, Mr. Chairman. I was president of the hospital in my native town for twenty-five years, and I know what it cost that hospital for alcohol. The great majority of our hospitals, particularly in the towns and smaller cities, are maintained very largely by private contributions. Now, the expense in connection with the provision of alcohol such as is referred to is very considerable. The tendency of the minister is to introduce more and more arbitrary legislation. In this case it is directed against the provinces to take away from them a right they have always possessed, and when later he institutes action under this section provided the bill passes he will find that he will have to abandcn'"it. In view of the facts, I think he should meet the reasonable request made in this connection. This is not the first time that the matter has been brought to his attention; I have discussed it with the minister on two or three occasions prior to this session, and I rather thought from the conversation I had with him that he would consider the matter favourably. I am sorry he has not; eventually he will be compelled to accede to the request.

I think the minister is
misinformed, because I am quite satisfied from my experience in dealing with hospitals that alcohol so seized in the past has been given to charitable institutions, that is hospitals.
I am certain it has.
I think the minister should consider the matter very seriously before making this regulation.

I must take the word of the Commisioner of Excise on this matter, for, as I say, I have no recollection of it myself! He says that so far as excisable liquor is concerned, that is liquor manufactured within the country, that has never been done. He does not answer for liquor that has been smuggled into the country, -as that would come under the Customs Act. After all, this is an amendment to the Excise Act, and I am assured by the commissioner that the practice of giving seized alcohol free to hospitals has never been followed.

I suppose the general
principle laid down by the government would apply, that inasmuch as the major number of

Winding-up Act
the provinces of confederation are not of the hon. minister's political views, alcohol could not be given to hospitals in those provinces, not even five cents' worth. Is that the idea?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Carried.

Section agreed to.
Section 19 agreed to.
Bill reported.
When shall the said bill be read a third time?
This day six months.
Next sitting.

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 53, to amend the Winding-Up Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
On section 1-By whom application for winding-up order may be made. '
Will the minister explain the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a very simple bill. Section 10 of the Winding-Up Act provides in what cases a winding-up order may be made. Section 11 specifies by whom the application may be made for a winding-up order. When a company is insolvent the law provides that a shareholder holding shares in the capital stock of the company to the amount of at least $500 may make application for winding up its affairs. To-day many corporations issue no par value stock, and the purpose of the amendment is to confer upon the holder of stock without nominal or par value-no par value stock-as nearly as .may be the same rights as are given by the existing section to the holders of shares having a par value; that is, if he holds at least five shares of no par value he may make application for a winding-up order.
I suppose the value of the shares cannot be determined except by actual sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Exactly.
Why are banks and insurance companies excepted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are already under the act.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 56, to amend the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This bill is
the usual one which we introduce each year for the purpose of withdrawing from forest reserves lands in the three prairie provinces, and this year in the province of British Columbia-lands which were included in forest reserves and which upon examination have been found fit for agricultural purposes. These lands are examined by officials of the department and recommended for withdrawal from the forest reserves. The bill also makes a considerable change in the area of the Rocky mountains and Jasper parks. It provides for an addition to these two parks of a considerable area at the southern boundary of Jasper park and the northern boundary of Rocky mountains park, where the two will now meet. This addition is very desirable from a scenic standpoint; as far as we know the area has no mineral value. On the other hand 1,364.46 square miles of rough, timbered, non-agricultural lands are being excluded from the Rocky mountains and Jasper parks. We are excluding the Spray lake and an adjacent area in the south; to the north of that there would appear to be minerals, particularly coal, along the eastern boundary of Rocky Mountains park and Jasper park. This change will affect the boundary lines of the two parks on the eastern side. So far as we know it will exclude everything that has any prospect of producing coal, except perhaps the area on the north or northeastern extremity of Jasper park, where there is undoubtedly some coal. There is a desirable country in that district consisting of very steep mountains and a narrow entrance through which the Canadian National railway passes; our road enters the park at Pocahontas, and it was thought desirable to make that the boundary of the park. Otherwise we have included non-mineralized areas.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The land will go to. the
province?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, the
forest reserves.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Has the province been consulted in regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes.

Forest Reserves and Parks Act

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Is it necessary to
have any portion of lands leased for community pastural purposes withdrawn in the same manner as these are? I refer particularly to lands fit for agricultural purposes and which at the present time are used as community pasture lands, leased through the department of agriculture of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In a forest
reserve ?

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Well that
would be a lease that we have turned over to the provincial government. That is not included in this.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
But is it necessary
to have it withdrawn in this way in order to make it available for homesteading purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, it
would be necessary to withdraw the lands from forest reserves if they were to be used for agricultural purposes. One or two leases have been turned over to the province for the purpose of community grazing, but they were leases of crown lands not included in forest reserves. Of course in nearly all the forest reserves we have been allowing stock to graze, and in some cases they have had leases. Very few leases however, are in existence. Nearly all the forest reserves which are fit for pasturage have been grazed.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The land I refer to is open prairie land and was at one time ranch property. I think it is dominion land and at the present time is leased to the provincial department of agriculture for community grazing purposes. A portion of the township consists of good agricultural land but so far the people have been unable to get the use of it. I was wondering if it would be necessary to have it included in a bill as in the present case.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: In connection with ranch land we have been consulting with the provincial departments of agriculture, and there have been withdrawals from leases for this purpose as well as from the forest reserves.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What progress has been made in connection with the surveys or resurveys of the proposed forest reserve area?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I cannot give any definite information to my hon. friend on that point. I can ascertain how much has
been done, but at the present time I cannot say what was accomplished last year. The section between the forest reserve and the park has been surveyed.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Have these provinces
been consulted in regard to the large block of land withdrawn from the Porcupine forest
reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is not
usual to consult the provinces in these matters. We send from our department men who have agricultural experience to examine the land, and if they report favourably, or report that the land is of more value for agricultural purposes than as forest reserves, we add these sections to the bill; we withdraw the land for agricultural purposes. I may say that we will not proceed to homestead these lands, particularly in Alberta, because the Alberta government have notified us that they do not purpose to continue homesteading. I believe they intend to sell these lands.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does that apply to
Alberta only?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I do not
think we have had any such communication from the government of Saskatchewan. It may be in the office; I would not like to say definitely. However, we will do nothing with these lands without consulting the provincial government as to what they desire to have done with them.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Does this bill make provision for the inclusion of any lands in the forest reserves except what the minister mentioned in regard to the national parks?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: No. We have been adding to the forest reserves by order in council, but it takes a statute to withdraw from them.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: These are all withdrawals?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister can
tell us how much land is in the forest reserves now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, I have
not that information at hand, but I oan get it.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is the purpose of the withdrawals, just in a sentence?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The inclusion in the forest reserves has been by order in council, and large areas were set aside as forest reserves without very minute examination. We are now making that minute exami-

Forest Reserves and Parks Act
nation, and after it 'has been made, if it appears that the land is more useful for agricultural purposes than for growing timber, we withdraw the land.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I notice there are several small portions here for Indian reserves. Is that being done in order to make better boundaries for these reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, in
nearly every case.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Could the minister tell us
how much land is covered by the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It is mentioned' in the bill. There are so many reserves involved, together with some very small parcels being withdrawn, that I have not computed the total amount.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: It happens that the representation from west of the great lakes on this side of the house is very Limited. It will not be as soon as the people have an opportunity to change it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
You are full of hope
to-night.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Not of hope but of
knowledge. May I direct attention to the fact that under this legislation, originally passed by this government, I think, orders in council can add to the forest reserves but orders in council cannot take away from them. The national parks of this country can be added to by order in council, but only by an act of parliament can they be limited. That applies to forest reserves. It will be observed that under the bill quarter-sections are being taken out; small areas are being taken out; one area of eight square miles is being excluded, and the whole matter has been gone into with a good deal of >care. These forest reserves will be vested in the provinces when the legislation has been ratified by the imperial parliament. The minister knows that at least one of the provinces suggested that a certain township which was opened for settlement the other day should not have been opened up, and they asked that that should not be done. The minister should lay on the table the correspondence which indicates that Alberta and Saskatchewan are satisfied with the proposed changes. I would expect that to be done; it is the right of the house to ask for it on behalf of the provinces here represented. The mere assertion that the provinces are satisfied is hardly sufficient. One of course accepts the statement of the minister, but there may be conditions imposed and exceptions made.
[Mr. C. A. Stewart.!

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I suggest to my hon. friend that the provinces have not been consulted about these withdrawals; I was speaking about the boundaries of the parks.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is the point I
desire to make. Do the provinces know that the forest reserves, which they believe they are to get under the natural resources bills, are to be lessened by these areas? I submit that they do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is right.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: If that is correct, I suggest that the minister do not proceed with this bill until the provinces have had an opportunity to say whether or not they will be content to have the areas they otherwise were to get lessened by what the minister is now taking away. Control of land is given to the Indian department in one case and to another department in another, while a further parcel is to be administered by this government as crown land in the right of the Dominion instead of in the right of the province. While this bill might be agreed to as far as the reference to the committee is concerned, it should not be passed until the provinces have signified that their interests have been adequately safeguarded. They should be given an opportunity to go over this bill, to plot the areas on the map, and see exactly what the facts are. For my part I have not had the time to examine the bill m detail. I did endeavour in a more or less casual way to look up the areas on a map, and it can be seen that they are very considerable; for instance, there is one area of 2,500 square miles. If my memory serves me aright, it will mean that about a million and a half acres of land which one of the provinces believed was to come under its control will now be withheld from it.

Forest Reserves and Parks Act

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister has not
followed my point. It may become a matter of the utmost importance to the governments of the provinces to know what the particular areas are; for they may be of strategic value from the provincial standpoint, and as the provinces are charged with the responsibility, in my judgment it would be well for the minister during the recess to have the matter formally presented to the provinces affected and to receive their approval. I cannot but think that in the circumstances this is a fair proposal, and one that the minister would be expected to act upon under other like conditions if he were concerned for the provinces and not for the Dominion. While my duty primarily is to the Dominion, I have a duty to the provinces as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
With the
exception of the additions to Indian reserves which, as I pointed out, are provided for in the agreement with the provinces, the whole of these lands remain with the provinces. All the land, with the exception of the additions to the Jasper and Rocky Mountains national parks, where we are adding a very small portion in comparison with what we are withdrawing from the parks, goes to the province of Alberta. It is well understood by the province that the boundaries are to be changed, which is done by agreement. There can be no complaint about that.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Where is the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The agreement as to boundaries.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: The resources agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, this is an agreement between the federal government and the province. For some two years the officers of both governments have been surveying the boundaries, and all the facts are well known to the Alberta government. With respect to the withdrawals of the remainder of the lands throughout the railway belt in British Columbia and in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, all these lands will be the property of the provincial governments, and I have stated that it is not my intention to make any disposition of any of these lands by way of homestead or otherwise, while they remain under the control of the federal government, without consulting the provinces. I should like to point out to my hon. friend that all this work has been performed by the officials of the Dominion government. They have examined these lands and recommended their withdrawal from the
forest reserve, and I am quite confident the provinces will be very glad to have this work performed. My hon. friend will agree with me that if land is of agricultural value, it should not be included within the area of a forest reserve, because there are large enough areas of land in all these provinces unfit for agricultural purposes which can remain within the boundaries of the forest reserve. Although I am quite satisfied that there will be no objection raised, I am perfectly willing to consult the province because I have no desire to have my hon. friend or any other hon. member of this house think that I am trying to take advantage of the provincial governments.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Now that the hon. minister has mentioned the matter, I will give him an illustration. The province of Saskatchewan and the Dominion of Canada made a bargain by which lands in the province within certain areas were to pass to the crown in right of the province. There was in that province an area known as t'he quarantine reserve; the minister opened it for settlement and it has been taken up. He received a request from the premier of Saskatchewan not to take this action, but it was disregarded. I brought the matter to his attention, acting upon a telegram sent to me, and the minister said that the notice had been given some time prior to that, in the month of March, and that the day fixed for entries at Moose Jaw was March 20. The premier of Saskatchewan asked merely that the date be extended for a time, but the minister telegraphed back that that could not be done and, as a matter of fact, that quarantine reserve has been homesteaded or preempted. What I was endeavouring at that time to point out to the minister with respect to the quarantine reserve, I say now about these forest reserves. Is there any assurance that the minister, having designated these lands as agricultural lands, will not do the same with them as he did with the quarantine reserve? It is all right to say that the provinces have agreed to this, but he offers no evidence of that; he says simply that they understand what is going on.

speechtext: That is the point I am endeavouring to make. Governments do not transact business of this character on mere word of mouth; there should be an undying record for the future, because governments are but ephemeral-very much so in this instance. May I impress upon the minister the seriousness of a matter of this kind? The minister has many things to care for and we cannot expect him to remember everything, but here vast areas are being set aside for agricultural purposes, some in Alberta, some in Saskatchewan, and lesser areas in Manitoba. All I have suggested to the minister is that we should not take those areas out of the operation of the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act unless there is some real assurance-not a Seven Sisters assurance -to the provinces that these matters will not bo dealt with by the minister while an agreement is pending. No minister is discharging his duty who merely says: Oh, well, it is understood. The department is in receipt of information that a serious case of devastation has occurred at the south end of Harrison lake, British Columbia. The action of the lake driven by high winds has created a very peculiar situation and unless some measures are taken very soon to protect property, considerable damage will be sustained by residents at this point. The district engineer reports as follows:
I have looked into this matter, and find that the shore of Harrison lake at the south end is eroding every year at high water for a distance of about 3,000 feet. The provincial government have started work on the west end of the portion that needs protection, and expect to complete about 1,000 feet this year with the $4,500 they have available for this work.
The method of protection is the placing of one-man rock on the bank, forming a slope of 45 degrees with the rock hand placed on the face, which will undoubtedly make an excellent protection and should last indefinitely.
When the provincial government finish this year (1929) there will be about 2,000 feet of protection required to prevent the balance of the road from being destroyed, which would cost about $9,000.
Then the other party is the provincial government only?
Yes.

The minister is here dealing with a matter I am sure every member of parliament has at times considered, namely, the extent to which the federal parliament should grant moneys where the matter concerned is an inland lake over which, and the areas of land contiguous thereto, the province exercises sole jurisdiction. What is the guiding principle? I realize it may sometimes be important that work of this character be done. But is this a case in which political considerations govern, or is there any other rule that can be applied and made effective? Is it the question whether or not the provincial government is Liberal that governs, or is it the size of the lake, the extent of the injury done by the waters, or what? Every hon. member knows that from time to time requests of a similar character have been made and denied. This hotel company has pretty powerful influence with the government and I should like the minister to explain the principle that governs; because I warn him that in the near future there will be presented to him many other claims far greater and far more deserving than that of the proprietors of the hotel on this lake-cases where the banks of rivers have been swept away by spring freshets and where assistance from this government-the provinces being unable to give it-has been sought in vain.	[DOT]

This contribution is being made to supplement a contribution made by the government of British Columbia. It is one of the cases which are, as my hon. friend has said, pretty numerous throughout the country where the devastation, as it is described by the engineer, is great. It was not considered that the province would repair the whole of the damage, and this contribution is being made as similar contributions have been made in the past.

What is the estimated cost complete? The amount is small, but a principle is involved in which everyone of us in the western provinces is greatly concerned, especially in the prairie provinces, along the banks of the Saskatchewan river and the Bow river. For instance, the city of Calgary found that the Bow river was cutting into its banks, with the result that lots that had been bought and sold as such have disappeared. Last spring on the Elbow river considerable property was simply swept away. A retaining wall would have saved that property, and there is a stronger claim for that retaining wall than any that can be made by the friends of the administration who own this hotel.

The same might be said of the banks of the Assiniboine and Red rivers. A portion of the town of Brandon was flooded a few years ago, and an effort was made to get the government to contribute something, but in vain.
Replying to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, the total cost will be $9,000, and we are bearing half the cost of completing the work.

Let us strip it of everything superfluous; this is just an ordinary case of political favouritism. As long as the principle is established, well and good, but let it be understood that that is what it is.
I know the whole property at Hot Springs, having seen it within a reasonably short time. The fact is that they wanted some money, the province is not giving them sufficient for their purpose, and so this government is going to give them some. I know how it goes on. Use sufficient pressure, carry on enough log rolling; represent what you are going to do when the time comes, and you will get it. But the time has come when this sort of thing should stop. This work could be done by day labour. It is under $5,000, and the eight-hour day could be applied, but only, of course, to those favourites who are able to get the work because they are supporters of the government.

I wish now to call the attention of the minister to the cable on Pictou island. Some little time ago I asked for some information which the minister was good enough to procure for me. This cable was first laid down in 1921, and during practically every year since it has been out of commission for some portion of the year. In March, 1922, nine months after it was laid down, the cable was out of commission for about three and one-half months; in 1923, for nine months; in 1924, about one and a half months, and the same in 1925; in 1927, it was out of commission again, also in 1928, and in 1929. The difficulty is that the cable was landed at a point on Pictou island where it is impossible to maintain cable communication. That difficulty has been repeatedly pointed out to the officers of the government. The cable is landed at a point where it is practically all rock, and the cable is worn through by the action of the waves and the surf rubbing and chafing it over the jagged rocks. The minister's officers will probably tell him, as they have told me, that the cable was destroyed by the action of the ice, but that could not have been the case

in the months of June, July, August and September. That is not the cause of the trouble. It is due entirely to the fact that the island end of the cable was landed at the wrong point. There is no trouble with the landing on the mainland end, and never has been. The difficulty always has been at the island end. I am told that no recommendation has been made for changing the landing place, but I would point out to the minister that more than one recommendation has been made to change the landing place on the island to a point further eastward, where it wovdd land on a sandy beach and where the present difficulty would not occur. Will the minister be good enough to tell me what is going to be done about it?

It is quite true that the cable has been out of commission at various times, for various reasons, and the reasons have been, I think fairly stated in the memorandum which my hon. friend has. That is the history of cables generally. Sometimes they are destroyed by ice shoves, sometimes by anchors of vessels catching them.
No, not in this case.

Oh yes; that is the main
reason, I am told. Cables are put out of business by many causes. So far as the location is concerned, considerable thought has been given to that matter, and we have had no recommendation from the departmental officials to change the site. That is the situation at the present time.

There may be many
reasons why cables in a general way go out of commission, but I am not discussing that. I am discussing this particular cable. I am not concerned about what suggestions have been given to the minister by his officers. I assert that this cable has broken down for the reason I have stated, and for no other reason. It is all very well for the minister to tell me that the cable has been carried away by vessels. That is not correct. The minister's information is at fault. I have been on the ground and have seen the condition of the cable more than once, and I also know what the opinions of the men on the island are, and they are quite capable of determining the cause of the trouble. The rough jagged rock surface at the point where the cable lands can at low water or half tide be seen quite easily. The cable itself is then easily visible; indeed the cable actually lands close to the public wharf head, and if the minister would look it over, he would see that it passes over a ledge of rock with a sharp, jagged surface, on which the waves and surf wash the cable back and

forth and wear it out. The obvious thing to do is to move the cable to a more suitable landing place a quarter of a mile distant, where that trouble will not occur. I defy anybody to successfully maintain anything different from what I have now stated.

I do not want to get into an argument with my hon. friend, whose judgment I esteem so very highly. I am surprised to hear him state with so much positiveness that the trouble is not as I have indicated. I would just refer him to the answer that was given him in reply to a question, on March 19, as to the cause of the cable ceasing to operate. I am sure that he has read it because he always pays great attention to the answers that he receives to his various questions.

My hon. friend has a

I take the opinion of the
officials of the department. I must confess that I still think they are right in spite of what my hon. friend says, and I have great respect for his statements.

breakage of this cable, why do the minister's officers persist in maintaining the landing place at the present point? Now, why not move the island landing place where the break has always been made? I would point out again that at the mainland end of the cable there has never been any obstruction.
